title: 2026 NFL season primer: Rule changes, notable games and more things to know entering Week 1
summary: Familiarize yourself with all the offseason changes ahead of kickoff
full_text:
Congratulations on making it through the NFL offseason! As the league embarks on a new campaign on Wednesday it is time to make sure everyone is up to speed on all the changes that unfolded over the last seven months.
In some ways, it is hard to believe it has been that long since the Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots and hoisted the Vince Lombardi Trophy. The NFL is such a year-round operation that it dominated headlines even in its quietest months.
There are a few new rules to learn before the Seahawks and Patriots return to the field in the first game of the 2026 season. There are also some schedule quirks unique to the upcoming campaign that everyone needs to be familiar with ahead of time. This year also brings a large batch of fresh uniforms and the opening of the doors to a new stadium.
Here are all of the changes to know ahead of the 2026 season.
Of the five playing rules changes the NFL approved at the Annual League Meeting in March, only four will actually apply to the 2026 season. The fifth would have permitted the league office to correct clear officiating mistakes in the event of an NFL Referees Association work stoppage, but a new collective bargaining agreement prevented the need for replacement officials in the first place. The following rule changes will, however, be active.
Additionally, during the final week of the preseason, the NFL and NFL Players Association voted to implement a new suspension rule for certain penalties . Any player who commits three offenses of any of the following penalties will receive a one-game suspension.
All players begin the 2026 season with a clean slate, but violations will carry forward into subsequent seasons. If a player commits just one violation, they will receive 50% of their fine back at the end of the campaign.
Half of the regular season's 18 weeks will feature an international game as the NFL expands its footprint outside the United States. For the first time, there will be nine games on foreign soil, the first of which comes right out of the gate as the second contest of the season. This year marks the inaugural Australia game, the third game in Brazil (and first in Rio de Janeiro) and the debut France game.
Here is the full international schedule:
Teams had better get used to this kind of travel, because the international slate is only going to get larger. The record of nine games abroad in one season will only stand for one year since the NFL is set to stage 10 such contests in 2027 .
Until 2026, only once in modern NFL history has the season started on a Wednesday. The NFL moved its standard Thursday opener up one day in 2012 to avoid a television ratings hit since former President Barack Obama was scheduled to speak at the Democratic National Convention on what would have otherwise been the first game day of the year.
It took 14 years for the league to schedule a second Week 1 Wednesday game. And this one is a doozy. It is a rematch of the 2026 Super Bowl which sends the New England Patriots all the way to the Pacific Northwest for a date with the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks.
Why the midweek kickoff? It all comes back to the Australia game. The league scheduled the Rams vs. 49ers showdown for Thursday, seemingly in an effort to give both teams time to adjust back to the Pacific Time Zone upon their return from a grueling trip Down Under. But the NFL also wanted to preserve its tradition of the defending Super Bowl champion being the first team to take the field. Thus, the Seahawks hit the turf one day prior to the international game.
Every game this year will be available to stream. Viewers will need just about every major streaming service to do so, though. That includes Netflix, which secured three additional games to its inventory as part of a renewed media rights contract it signed in May. The Christmas Day game now becomes a doubleheader, and Netflix will also carry the league's first Thanksgiving Eve game.
These games will be available only on Netflix as part of the streamer's expanded package:
More major broadcast changes come as part of ESPN's acquisition of NFL Network. The biggest development in this regard is the discontinuation of "Monday Night Football" doubleheaders. ESPN returned that inventory to the NFL, which then redistributed games to other partners.
In turn, there are four games on CBS, Fox and NBC that fall in non-traditional windows:
Some of football's best players will suit up for new teams in 2026, including reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett , whose trade to the Rams shocked the NFL and solidified Los Angeles as the Super Bowl front-runner. He is one of the numerous familiar faces in new places this year.
Kirk Cousins ( Raiders ), Kyler Murray (Vikings), Malik Willis ( Dolphins ), Geno Smith ( Jets ) and Tua Tagovailoa (Falcons) are the quarterbacks who will start for new teams.
A bevy of blockbuster trades sent stars to fresh destinations. In addition to the Garrett deal, the Rams also traded for cornerback Trent McDuffie . The Bengals acquired defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence . A quartet of standout receivers have new homes with A.J. Brown heading to the Patriots, DJ Moore being scooped up by the Bills, Jaylen Waddle landing with the Broncos and Michael Pittman finding himself on the Steelers.
In free agency, the Bengals loaded up on defense with Boye Mafe , Jonathan Allen and Bryan Cook bolstering a unit that needs to improve significantly in 2026. Star edge rusher Trey Hendrickson signed with the Ravens after they nixed their trade for Maxx Crosby . And reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III departed Seattle to become the leader of the Chiefs ' run game.
That is in addition to the 10 head coaching changes, which tied the league record for a single offseason:
The new Highmark Stadium opens for regular-season business on Thursday, Sept. 17 when the Bills play host to the Lions. That Week 2 contest opens a new era after Buffalo moved from its old home, where it played from 1973-2025.
EverBank Stadium is in the midst of renovations, which will limit the attendance at Jaguars home games. The reduced capacity of about 43,500 fans will be the league's smallest. The Jaguars will then play their home games in Orlando in 2027 as their Jacksonville venue undergoes the final stages of construction.
This is also the final year for the Titans in Nissan Stadium, which will be replaced by a new Nissan Stadium in 2027.
An expansion of the "Rivalries" uniform series gives new threads to every team in the AFC South and NFC North this year. Half of the league now owns a set of these alternate ensembles.
Additional alternates will make their debuts in Buffalo and Tampa Bay: The Bills' new "Nickel City" outfit and the return of the all-pewter Buccaneers uniform. The Ravens, Bills, Jets and Commanders also have new alternate helmets.
The biggest changes come for the following five teams, who unveiled new sets of primary uniforms.
Authentic, Fast, Timeless pic.twitter.com/mUu516fq1g
look at the details 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/I75lHKh4Hv
Threaded with Greatness. pic.twitter.com/2t1vqqf0lt
Titans of Tennessee pic.twitter.com/f7MEinwKcb
Without further ado... pic.twitter.com/0lOyf0wo20
In 2026, the NFL bids farewell to the Pro Bowl . The week between the conference championship games and Super Bowl will no longer feature any all-star festivities as the league announced in August that the "Pro Bowl Games" will not return for another installment. Although the game (or most recently, the skills competitions) is a thing of the past, 88 players will still receive Pro Bowl honors at the end of each season. Also, since there is no physical game, there will no longer be any alternates selected to the Pro Bowl roster, either.
author: Carter Bahns

title: Predicting the race for the No. 1 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft: Dolphins, Jets among five contenders
summary: Securing the No. 1 pick requires enduring a miserable season, but the reward could be a franchise-changing quarterback from the 2027 draft class
full_text:
Every regular season, there are two battles in the NFL standings . One is the postseason race, and the other is the competition for the No. 1 overall draft pick. The winners of those fights have plenty of reason to feel good about themselves, but the one who secures the top pick in the draft should only take so much pride in it. For as much value as there is in selecting first, you have to be the worst of 32 teams to do so.
Securing the first pick this year should be viewed as even more of a potential franchise-turning point than in other years. The 2027 quarterback class has been ballyhooed for some time now as a loaded crop with perhaps multiple future elite franchise signal-callers. Having the choice of the bunch is a luxury, even if it means the road to get there came with a whole lot of losses.
Here are the five teams that figure to compete the toughest for the No. 1 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft .
Jeff Hafley is a good coach who, like he did at Boston College, finds himself in a rough situation. This is a developmental year for the NFL's youngest roster, and Hafley should be trusted to deliver some promise on the defensive side of the ball. But with such an empty cupboard across the roster's entirety, it would require a masterclass in coaching to even pull the Dolphins out of the AFC East's basement.
Even if Malik Willis hits as a full-time starting quarterback, there just is not enough talent around him to maximize that breakout. De'Von Achane can shoulder a heavy load, but the wide receiver group is quite clearly the league's worst .
The schedule is a grind, which does no favors for an undermanned team. Catching the Jets twice helps, but battling a pair of Super Bowl contenders in the Bills and Patriots should account for four losses. Drawing the entire NFC North and AFC West hurts, too, considering those divisions are deep with likely playoff squads.
There is some real skill position talent in the desert this year between Jeremiyah Love , Trey McBride and perhaps even a breakout-ready Marvin Harrison Jr . The defense has a couple of pieces to like in Josh Sweat and Budda Baker . The roster as a whole simply falls well short of the extremely high NFC West standard, though, which sets the Cardinals up for another long season.
Chalk up six division losses. Add in projected defeats to the myriad of other projected postseason contenders, and that column fills up extremely quickly. There is some runway at the end of the year to potentially build momentum heading into 2027 with the Jets, Saints and Vikings on the slate from Weeks 15-17, but even a win or two in that stretch might not be enough to keep the Cardinals from the bottom of the league standings.
The bottom should not fall out from underneath the Jets, because the front office made enough personnel moves defensively to raise the floor from what was an abysmal 2025 season. That does not guarantee upward mobility, though. This is a team that won a mere three games in Aaron Glenn's first campaign, and another slow start could see New York move on. The franchise has to ask itself whether Glenn is the one they want to oversee a rookie quarterback's development in 2026.
An in-season coaching change would be a forward-facing move that likely comes at the expense of wins in 2026. But even if Glenn holds onto his job, there is no reason to believe the Jets will flourish. Sure, there is young talent on the offense, but it is difficult to trust Geno Smith to utilize it at this stage of his career. And for all Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick accomplished over their combined 22 years in the league, veterans whose best football is behind them can only do so much in elevating the defense to a new tier.
A ferocious defense won the Browns a couple of games last year. It often kept them competitive in losses, too. But Myles Garrett is gone. Regression is coming; the question is how much. Perhaps Jared Verse limits the impact of Garrett's departure. The secondary is still strong, and linebacker projects as a strength. The problem is that Cleveland cannot afford for its defense to take even a slight step backward, because the offense could be truly miserable.
The young building blocks are enticing. The quarterback situation remains the league's worst. Last year, that equation amounted to five wins and the No. 6 draft pick (before the Browns traded it to the Chiefs ). It could amount to even less in 2026, because Deshaun Watson is simply that bad.
Cleveland is a middle-of-the-road quarterback away from being a respectable team. That has seemingly been the story for decades, but this time, there actually is a lot to be excited about at the other positions. The Browns could have their pick of signal-callers in the next draft, and they had better not mess it up again.
Everything on paper suggests the Titans should be breakout candidates. They hold a second-year, former No. 1 overall pick quarterback and a promising young receiving unit. They boast arguably the best interior defensive lineman in football in Jeffery Simmons . The head coach-offensive coordinator tandem of Robert Saleh and Brian Daboll could be a terrific pairing.
What they showed in training camp and in preseason games, however, was not worthy of optimism. Ward went just 13-for-24 for 126 yards and no touchdowns in two preseason appearances. Saleh's starting defense had a couple of concerning lapses, most notably in the game against the Seahawks wherein Seattle's No. 2 offense logged a 36-yard passing touchdown and practice-squad running back Jacardia Wright broke loose for a 69-yard rushing score.
If the preseason was any indication of what is to come, the Titans will find themselves adding even more early-first-round assets to their young core. There will also be questions about whether Ward is fit to be that unit's ringleader.
author: Carter Bahns

title: 2026 NFL coach hot seat tiers: Zac Taylor, Dan Quinn among those feeling the heat
summary: Ahead of the season, we assess where every coach lands on the hot seat scale
full_text:
The NFL is very much a "what have you done for me lately?" enterprise, and that especially applies to head coaches. A down year can put some of the most highly regarded coaches in some hot water, and two down years in a row might earn them a pink slip. It differs from team to team, owner to owner and front office to front office, but the coaching carousel is busy every offseason. Last year's 10 coaching changes were especially high, but the year before, there were eight, and the year before that, there were seven.
We can expect at least a handful next year, too, whether it's via an in-season firing or an exit after the season. And while some might be expected, others won't be. Entering last year, it would have been impossible to predict Mike Tomlin stepping down as Steelers coach and John Harbaugh getting fired by the Ravens .
With one day until the 2026 season kicks off, we assess the five coaches with the hottest hot seats, as well as a few who could be a potential surprise split come season's end.
From this observer's perspective, Steichen has done a really good job when he had even a playable quarterback. He was 17-17 through two years with Anthony Richardson , Gardner Minshew and Joe Flacco as his quarterbacks and then surged to a 8-2 start last year with a healthy Daniel Jones . Then Jones popped up on the injury report with a fracture in his leg before tearing his Achilles a few weeks later. Last year's Colts finished 8-9.
Steichen's offensive smarts shouldn't be in doubt, but the circumstances around him aren't exactly favorable. Chris Ballard is about as "hot seat" as it gets for a GM considering the Colts have won one playoff game since he took over the role in 2017, and that postseason win was in 2018. Jones is coming off a torn Achilles, and even though he has looked good, time will tell if he's back. The AFC South has gotten much stronger with the Texans and Jaguars surging last year, and the AFC as a whole figures to be a dogfight.
If Ballard is gone, is Steichen gone? If Jones struggles, is Steichen gone? Even if Jones and the offense as a whole are good, is the defense good enough to support playoff aspirations? The Colts could look to start anew, and if they do, Steichen would immediately be an in-demand option next offseason, similar to how Kevin Stefanski got the Falcons job this offseason shortly after being fired by the Browns .
Glenn's 2025 was, predictably, a disaster. The offense was awful as Justin Fields struggled. New York started Fields, Tyrod Taylor and, by the end of the season, undrafted rookie Brady Cook under center. Likely more disappointing for Glenn, a former cornerback and defensive coordinator, though, was his defense. The Jets became the first team ever to finish a season without an interception , allowed the highest passer rating in the NFL and finished 30th in defensive expected points added per play. There were constant breakdowns everywhere.
This offseason, New York focused on getting a ton of steady veterans in the door, not to lift the team to playoff contention, but to simply raise the floor. Still, there are worries. Glenn fired eight different assistant coaches, including both coordinators. However, he took nearly a month after the season ended to fire offensive coordinator Tanner Engstrand, meaning the Jets had already missed out on even attempting to lure in some of the more sought-after play callers available. They eventually landed on Frank Reich, whose last two NFL offenses were among the worst in the league. The last time we saw him in the NFL, he didn't even survive one season as Carolina's head coach in 2023. He was out of football in 2024 and Stanford's interim coach in 2025.
The Jets are loaded with draft capital -- three first-rounders in 2027 -- and in need of a quarterback. They will also need to restock a defense currently featuring veterans on short deals. GM Darren Mougey could look to pair his new signal-caller with a new, offensive-minded head coach. At the very least, Glenn's team must look competent. He can get a pass, somewhat, for last year. That won't be the case again in 2026.
In four seasons in Tampa, Todd Bowles has recorded between eight and 10 wins every year. It looked like the Buccaneers were ready to leave that middle ground last year when they started 6-2, but they melted down over the second half of the year.
Bowles hangs his hat on the defensive side of the ball, but Tampa Bay was 20th in scoring defense last year, the worst mark by a Bowles-coached defense since his 2018 Buccaneers. On the offensive side of the ball, he's on his fifth coordinators in five years. He fired Byron Leftwich after his first year, lost Dave Canales to the Panthers ' coaching job in 2024, lost Liam Coen to the Jaguars' coaching job in 2025 and fired Josh Grizzard earlier this year. Now, it's Zac Robinson , who was most recently with the Falcons. That hire is crucial for Bowles' future.
More than anything, though, the Buccaneers feel like a team in transition. Baker Mayfield is playing out the last year of his deal without an extension. Mike Evans is gone. Lavonte David is gone. There's a influx of young defensive talent, including Rueben Bain Jr . and Josiah Trotter in the first and second round, respectively, a strong offensive line and several intriguing players around Mayfield. It's a good -- not great -- roster in a bad division. Anything less than a return to the playoffs and a much-improved defense would have Bowles feeling the heat.
After leading Washington to a 12-5 record and its first NFC Championship game in 30+ years in 2024, Quinn went 5-12 last year. Injuries were a major factor, but Quinn admitted the standard slipped, too.
Quinn inherited a rough situation (really rough, in fact), and the roster still has significant holes in terms of top-end talent and depth. Laremy Tunsil's torn triceps didn't help. The 2026 season features a brutal start of at the Eagles , at the Cowboys and against the Seahawks , and if Washington starts slowly, the heat will really turn up on Quinn.
On one hand, Josh Harris has a history of being patient. As 76ers owner, he oversaw "The Process." On the other hand, the Commanders have failed to put a quality enough product around Jayden Daniels . Quinn is betting big on offensive coordinator David Blough and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones -- both first-time play callers -- to elevate their respective units. It could be argued that a bounce-back year, even if it doesn't result in a playoff berth, would be enough for him to stay another year. But even that is no certainty.
There are simply no more excuses. After all, as Joe Burrow said in May : "We have everything we need in that locker room. We just gotta go and make it happen."
Cincinnati finally got serious about investing on defense, trading for Dexter Lawrence and signing Boye Mafe , Bryan Cook and Jonathan Allen. Burrow's entire offensive line is back, as are Ja'Marr Chase , Tee Higgins and Chase Brown . Taylor is trying his best to diversify the attack by getting Burrow under center more, an aspect that could, hypothetically, help ... if it goes smoothly. Burrow has never exactly loved the concept, but it should be a boon for the run game.
Taylor is the only AFC North coach not in his first season. The Ravens, Browns and Steelers all moved on from coaches who had previously had major success. Harbaugh and Tomlin were both Super Bowl winners. Stefanski won two Coach of the Year awards. Taylor remains despite having accomplished neither. If this year isn't the year to return to the postseason -- the drought is up to three years now -- Taylor might not return, period.
author: Zachary Pereles

title: Prisco's NFL Week 1 Power Rankings: Jaguars, Cowboys deserve attention; Rams' super team too good to be true
summary: Pete Prisco shares his first Power Rankings of the 2026 NFL season, and he's ready for the critics to unleash their fury
full_text:
NFL Week One Power Rankings often become fodder for jokes at the end of the season. That's because we usually have no idea what's about to take place in the wild, crazy NFL. Yet as we head into this season, it's all about the Los Angeles Rams .
Why are the other 31 teams even playing? I mean the Rams are the chic, trendy pick to win it all. They are star-laden, with the reigning MVP at quarterback in Matthew Stafford , along with defensive stars in Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald , who came out of retirement after sitting out two seasons. They can't be stopped or blocked.
Most have the Rams in the Super Bowl . I do not, even though they have so much talent. It's just too obvious. The team that is crowned in August usually doesn't win it all.
Plus, their division is brutal. Let's not forget the Super Bowl-champion Seattle Seahawks are in that division. The Seahawks start the season at No. 1 in my Power Rankings because the champs always start at the top. The Rams are second.
Will the Seahawks finish in the top spot and repeat? Not the way I see it, but they will be a deep playoff team.
My picks to play in the Super Bowl are the Dallas Cowboys and the Jacksonville Jaguars . You've already had good laughs about that one when I released it last week. Keep laughing. Talk to me in February.
The Jaguars are third in my rankings to open the season with the Cowboys fifth. When I made the Super pick last week, people said I was either crazy, on drugs or just too damn old -- many in nastier tones than that.
I just think the Jaguars, who won 13 games last year, will be a better team this time around. The Cowboys were already good on offense, but now will be much better on defense with a new coordinator in Christian Parker and a lot of new, talented faces.
The Miami Dolphins start at the bottom and I think they will stay there for a much of the season. This season is about building for the Dolphins, not wins. If Miami wins four games, it will be a successful first season for new coach Jeff Hafley.
So print this out and keep it. I guarantee based on past history that you will get a lot of laughs from these rankings come December. That happens every year.
We think we know. We really don't.

title: Exactly how this Cardinals’ receiver group is shaping up
summary: The Arizona Cardinals are dotting their “i’s” and crossing all the “t’s” as they prepare to play their first game of the season this weekend against the Los Angeles Chargers. This is an exciting time for both the coaching staff, the players, and the Cardinals fanbase.   RELATED: CARDINALS EXTEND MICHAEL WILSON This new offensive […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - NOVEMBER 10: Marvin Harrison Jr #18 and Michael Wilson #14 of the Arizona Cardinals run up field against the New York Jets at State Farm Stadium on November 10, 2024 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Norm Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals are dotting their “i’s” and crossing all the “t’s” as they prepare to play their first game of the season this weekend against the Los Angeles Chargers. This is an exciting time for both the coaching staff, the players, and the Cardinals fanbase. RELATED: CARDINALS EXTEND MICHAEL WILSON This new offensive system is the headline of this year’s team. New head coach Mike LaFleur has taken his experience under similar systems used with the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers. Does this mean that the Cardinals will have the offensive firepower of their division foes LA and SF? Yes and no. Yes, it is designed similarly, with a lot of schemes, player personnel, and traits the same. No, in that this doesn’t happen overnight. But this offense is loaded with talent. That is, on paper. It all starts with the offensive line and the talent of the quarterback. We will see if both of these boxes become checked as games fall off the calendar. The true test of the new offense is how the receiver room is utilized. Let’s do a deep dive. “X” receiver The X receiver lines up wide from the offensive line. Back in the day, it was referred to as the “split end.” This position is responsible for running a complete route tree, having good moves, physicality, and the ability to get downfield. Marv Harrison (6’-3”, 220 pounds) is the Cardinals’ X receiver. It is what he played in college, and last year’s coaching staff – along with LaFleur’s guys – have kept him there. Harrison had a ton of success in the X at Ohio State, so why relocate him and attempt to teach him a new job? Just imagine if Harrison can take a huge leap this year. Name a receiver award in college, and that hardware became a fireplace mantelpiece for his household. There are plenty of questions regarding Harrison, and it all begins with his durability. He spent his entire career at all levels without ever having any major injuries, but last year he was in and out of the lineup. If he can remain upright, he can become a very valuable tool in this offense. This position typically remains isolated all game. In LaFleur’s system, Harrison must be highly versatile and will be moved around from side to side quite a bit. This is because of tactical responsibilities. One of these is the ability to absorb and fight off physicality from the outside cornerback, who can jam Harrison as soon as the ball is snapped. His job has no cushion against aggressive press coverage, and he has to be able to beat a jam. The X has the ability to use the sideline to his benefit. The X must be a good downfield blocker. Harrison is considered a willing and capable blocker, although this is not his strongest asset. While this offense will use quite a bit of 12 and 13 personnel, this will often leave the X isolated in man coverage for his number to be called, or simply running the decoy on a clear-out route for another receiver underneath. The main job of the X is to win those isolated man matchups. Harrison showed in college that that is his style of play anyway. “Z” receiver This is where it gets interesting. Last year’s sensation in this offense, Michael Wilson (6’-2”, 213 pounds) is the Z receiver. This position is different from last year’s offensive scheme. Back in the day, this was referred to as the “flanker.” Look at the Los Angeles Rams. The Z is Puka Nacua. Look at the Seattle Seahawks. Their Z is Cooper Kupp. Typically, the Z receiver is the secondary option, but in LaFleur’s offense, it is the engine that sparks the passing game. The Z is a step off the line of scrimmage as another outside receiver and is able to go in motion. Part of the scheme for the Z is that it heavily utilizes play-action concepts that strike the intermediate portions of the field. This helps the offensive line because plays don’t take that long to develop, and the ball is out pretty quickly. Now, it does require a receiver who isn’t afraid to run crossing routes and deal with hard-hitting safeties. As the Z the past three seasons, Nacua had 160, 106, and 166 targets, and 1,486, 990, and 1,715 yards, respectively. And who was Nacua’s coach? LaFleur. Slot receiver This position sits inside its own little pocket outside of either side’s offensive tackle, or if a tight end is lined up. He must be a step off the line and have another receiver on his outside shoulder. He is another guy who will often go into motion and run the ball on the jet sweep. Usually, this is a smaller receiver. For now, Kendrick Bourne (6’-1”, 205 pounds) is playing the slot. Tyreek Hill is a great example who perfectly fills this role by getting up to speed before he turns upfield and has a good running start, often just blowing by his defender. And while Bourne isn’t running in the 4.3 range, his time in the 40 was 4.68, so he doesn’t have that flat-out speed, but he does have quickness. This is a player who rarely gets jammed at the line and doesn’t have the sideline to work with or help him out with bad throws. Bourne is used to the short passing game, which is what the slot was invented for. All it takes is to fool just one defender, and either the center of the field or a soft zone towards the sideline is what he is working for. More than the other two positions, the slot guy must be able to create separation. And after he has gotten some space between himself and the defender, he must be able to defend himself against a head-hunting safety. At times, Bourne will be asked to take it deep, usually in center field. By taking his routes down the middle of the field, he has the advantage of knowing which direction he will break off his route. The depth There will be some four-receiver sets, but only once in a while. But this offense would rather stick another tight end on the field than four pass catchers. When it does happen, most likely you will see Simi Fehoko (6’-4”, 225 pounds), who is the backup to Wilson, as WR4. Two players who should get some snaps are Jalen Brooks (6’-1”, 205 pounds) and the rookie, Reggie Virgil (6’-3”, 187 pounds). Devin Duvernay (5’-10”, 202 pounds) is also listed in the receiver room, but most likely he will be strictly a kickoff and punt returner. Brooks is the guy who might be able to strip away some snaps from Bourne. He has an uncanny ability to get open in deep soft zones and is fearless about being around defenders. He will take hits and secure the catch extremely well. The coaches are very high on the rookie Virgil. But just remember, it is a very deep room. And he is in his first year, so his best friend is patience. This entire group for the past two years pretty much was reliant on the development of Harrison, who was taken with the fourth overall pick and was expected to become the next Jerry Rice and blow up the league. But with the development of Wilson last year, and the experience of Bourne being signed away from the 49ers (who run this same offense) and the preseason success of both Brooks and Virgil, the Cardinals won’t have to rely on Harrison so much this year. If he continues to get injured, the offense is no longer decimated by his absence. There are guys now who can become plug-and-play, and the beat goes on. If Harrison can remain vertical, if Wilson can grow his game even further, and if Bourne can fill his role with his nine years of experience, this will give the Cardinals what they have been missing for many, many years since the glory days of Larry Fitzgerald. A balanced passing attack. The Cardinals open Week 1 on Sunday, September 13, on the road against the Chargers. Kickoff is at 4:25 p.m.(Eastern) and will be broadcast on CBS.

title: Who is the “Face of the Cardinals”?
summary: Anytime you see a network plug an upcoming NFL game, they always display a featured player as part of the enticement to get viewers. Usually, it is the quarterback since that is normally the most recognized face on their team. As an example, teams like the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams are an easy […]
full_text: Simi Fehoko #80, Jacoby Brissett #7, Marvin Harrison Jr. #18 and Michael Wilson #14 (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Anytime you see a network plug an upcoming NFL game, they always display a featured player as part of the enticement to get viewers. Usually, it is the quarterback since that is normally the most recognized face on their team. As an example, teams like the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams are an easy sell with the photos of Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford, respectively. RELATED: 2026 DRAFT CLASS NEEDS TO COME THROUGH Sometimes, the networks will show a trio of players so that they can feature other guys who usually are the ones who score points or garner a huge number of sacks. Yes, defenders have been featured before, but there are few. Which begs the question: Who is the “Face of the Cardinals”? Let’s examine some candidates. QB Jacoby Brissett Well, certainly the quarterback for the franchise should be considered. However, Brissett has primarily been named the backup quarterback for the majority of his NFL career. Yes, he is now the Cardinals’ starting QB, which should fill a role with the popular vote. And networks love quarterbacks. Brissett is a pro's pro. Locker room loves him. — DJ White (@DJWhite12184) September 7, 2026 But if he remains the starting QB, which is currently expected, he will need to dump that former self when he was an annual backup for the majority of his 11-year career. He has played in 101 games with just 65 starts. He did have a stretch with the Indianapolis Colts where he was their starter for two seasons, and he started the first 11 games for the Cleveland Browns in the 2022 season while the franchise was waiting for Deshaun Watson to finish out his 11-game suspension. But when that expired, Brissett warmed up the bench. In order to become “The Face” of the Cardinals, he will need to ball out and play at a Pro Bowl level all season. He was voted the offensive Captain, so that’s a start. RB Jeremiyah Love Back in the day, running backs were the most popular position for fans. And a team made sure they had an Emmitt Smith, Barry Sanders, Eric Dickerson, LaDainian Tomlinson, or Walter Payton who would routinely receive 25-30 carries a game. Running backs carried the ball. They scored near the goal line. They could break big plays and take on bigger athletes such as linebackers. They got the reputation of being the bellcow for the offense and are exciting to watch when they grind out nine yards with three guys on them. . @JeremiyahLove moves different 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/pPgQvEwg95 — Arizona Cardinals (@AZCardinals) May 12, 2026 Can Love rekindle that long-gone tradition? In today’s game, almost every offense features at least two backs, and sometimes three. Such is the case for the Cardinals, who will use Tyler Allgeier to supplement Love. And who knows, as soon as James Conner returns, how many carries any of these RBs will actually get. Love was the #3 overall pick in this year’s NFL Draft, and he is a running back from a major college such as Notre Dame. All the boxes are checked for him to eventually be named “The Face.” WRs Marv Harrison/Michael Wilson Everyone loves the guys who catch passes and score touchdowns. These can be electric plays and, of course, advance the scoreboard. In college, name a receiver award, and Harrison won it. And he had a production season in his rookie campaign. But last year was full of injuries, which means so far his professional career has been a roller coaster. He came to the Cardinals with the term “generational” hanging all over him. Wilson is a former third-round pick, and all anybody expected out of him was to complement guys like Harrison. Going into Week 6 last year, he had very few targets and even less receptions. But once Kyler Murray became injured and Jacoby Brissett took over, his numbers increased. He ended up with highs in every category of his career, including getting over the 1,000-yard plateau. Now, he has a new huge contract, so the franchise is accepting that he can be “The Face” of the franchise, right? TE Trey McBride It is conceivable for a tight end to gather the limelight. Look at Travis Kelce with the Chiefs and George Kittle with the San Francisco 49ers. They show their tight ends frequently as featured players. And McBride is more of a large receiver than a traditional tight end. He has the background to become a league leader. His numbers were decent as a rookie. But into his second season, somebody figured out this dude could catch, and he had 106 targets, 81 receptions for 825 yards, 42 first-down conversions, and three touchdowns. The last two years, he has had 147 and 169 targets for 1,146 yards and 1,239 yards, respectively. IN 2025, McBride broke the single-season record for receptions by a tight end when he grabbed his 117 th catch in late December, beating the mark of 116 catches. For McBride to be considered an elite NFL player, he will need more than his two Pro Bowls and to gather more yardage each season. A guy like Kelce has had six seasons where he gained over 1,000 yards. He owns 11 Pro Bowls. OT Paris Johnson, Jr. Can an offensive lineman become the icon as well? But why Johnson? He hasn’t been on the roster that long and has yet to get his first Pro Bowl. So, there’s that. The #AZCardinals have picked up the fifth-year option on LT Paris Johnson Jr., source says. That’s just over $19 million for the 2027 season for the 2023 sixth-overall pick with more surely coming eventually via a new deal at some point. pic.twitter.com/TSxLFDvFtO — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) April 16, 2026 His mission this year is not to have to be compared repeatedly to some of the greatest Cardinals’ linemen in franchise history. Plus, with the three new offensive linemen, he has to remain healthy and stay on the field and not miss many practices or playing time. Doesn’t durability get any votes? S Budda Baker Now we are talking. However, networks don’t usually pick defensive players, and if they do, it is usually a guy like Myles Garrett who will have a storage shed full of sacks each season. So, Baker is working against traditional aspects in network TV. But the veteran safety certainly has plenty of cred going into his 10 th NFL season. Being named to the “NFL All-Rookie Team,” 8 Pro Bowls (including the last seven consecutively), two-time First Team All-Pro, two-time Second Team All-Pro, and winning the Rooney Award is a terrific career in just nine seasons. Had 164 tackles in 2024. This just might be our man. He certainly isn’t a “look at me” type of player. He simply does his job and gets back into the defensive huddle. He isn’t on the cover of Sports Illustrated and doesn’t boast about his stats. “The Face” hasn’t been a defender for quite some time, and perhaps Baker can just slide into the position. Remember the diving interception against Jacksonville last year? He is usually a defensive Captain, and was again voted to this distinction again for 2026. DE Josh Sweat It might seem unfair to consider a guy like Sweat, in that he has only played one year for the Cardinals. But let’s go a bit deeper. Sweat has played seven years in the league and came to Arizona last year to be reunited with his former defensive coach Jonathan Gannon. A lot of controversy with him during the offseason about whether he wanted to remain with the Cardinals now that Gannon has moved on. But we will see, as he is under contract. As far as a pass rusher, he is pretty much it. Last season he had a high in career sacks with 12.5 with 17 QB hits, 13 tackles for loss, 2 batted passes, 4 forced fumbles, 1 fumble recovery, 7 knockdowns, 9 hurries, 28 pressures, and zero missed tackles. If Sweat was named “The Face,” his numbers justify it so far.

Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Falcons fans and fans across the country. Although Tua Tagovailoa was selected as the starter against Pittsburgh, it’s inevitable that Michael Penix Jr. will take over as the signal caller at some point. Evidence from training camp and preseason suggests Tagovailoa is merely a placeholder as Penix Jr. gets healthy. From his inability to push the ball downfield to maneuver around the pocket, the former Dolphin’s glaring limitations will make it difficult to maintain faith in his ability to maxmize the offense’s capabilities. A daunting road matchup to start the season will only increase the conversations about Penix Jr. taking over. After facing the Panthers in their home opener, a short week to Green Bay may raise the pressure even further among a fan base that has endured incompetent quarterback play for too long. An extended week to prepare to face their biggest rival may be an ideal time to make the switch. Performance will ultimately determine how the coaching staff moves forward, but it’s hard to envision the Falcons getting off to a winning start in September. title: Falcons news: Gervon Dexter on his fit in Jeff Ulbrich’s defense and more
summary: Good morning Falcoholics! As strange as it feels to say on a Wednesday, the NFL season kicks off tonight, and that means the Falcons’ first game of the season is just a few days away. I’ll be in Flowery Branch today for Falcons practice and media availability, and I’ll keep you posted on all of […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 04: Gervon Dexter Sr. #99 of the Chicago Bears and Grady Jarrett #50 of the Chicago Bears celebrate after sacking Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions (not pictured) in the third quarter at Soldier Field on January 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning Falcoholics! As strange as it feels to say on a Wednesday, the NFL season kicks off tonight, and that means the Falcons’ first game of the season is just a few days away. I’ll be in Flowery Branch today for Falcons practice and media availability, and I’ll keep you posted on all of the developments in the Feed right here on The Falcoholic . The schedule and players/coaches available are always subject to change, but on Wednesday we expect to hear from Kevin Stefanski around noon, Bijan Robinson is expected to address the media about an hour later, and then Tua Tagovailoa will take the podium after practice, around 3:55 p.m. We heard from brand-new Falcon Gervon Dexter on Monday, and today’s Opening Drive walks through some of his more interesting comments. In our community spotlight, I’d forgotten all about Dexter’s RAS score , but it’s worth revisiting. And don’t miss today’s Falcoholic Question of the Day : How many games do you think Tua will start this season, and why? Falcons Opening Drive: Grady Jarrett told Gervon Dexter he’s going to love Atlanta I miss Grady Jarrett, and I’m sure I’m not the only one. Well, Grady still loves Atlanta and the Falcons, and he said as much to his now-former Bears teammate Gervon Dexter, who was traded to the Falcons back on Aug. 30, 2026 . Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Dexter was asked if he got any Atlanta advice from Grady, and he said Grady came to him. “Grady hit me up and told me I was gonna love it here, and the people were great,” Dexter said. Grady Jarrett sounds like he hasn’t changed a bit since signing with the Bears after he was released by the Falcons in 2024 . “Grady’s … a leader, a crazy leader,” Dexter said. “I’d tell a lot of the young guys coming in, if you want to know what to do, look at Grady, ‘cause he’s always in the right place, you know what I mean? He’s always on time. He don’t do a lot of stuff wrong, so Grady’s a great guy. He helped me a lot last year.” Another Bears-Falcons connection for Dexter is general manager Ian Cunningham, who helped build the team the Bears took to the postseason last year. Dexter said it meant a lot, after Cunningham was part of the crew who drafted him, to land here with a familiar face in the front office. And Dexter thinks he’s a great fit for Jeff Ulbrich’s defense, because he’s “big, fast, strong,” and he loves to be able to “just go” out on the field. Dexter joined some fellow former Florida Gators in Atlanta — right tackle Jawaan Taylor, cornerback C.J. Henderson, and obviously Kyle Pitts Jr. are all Florida alums. And the Falcons ended up with just two Georgia Bulldogs on the 53-man roster ( Jalon Walker remains on injured reserve after tearing his ACL during training camp , and Cash Jones is on Atlanta’s practice squad), but that’s more than enough for Dexter. “They got a lot of Dawgs here,” Dexter said, laughing. “I’m not okay with that.” Now, let’s move on to the Falcons coverage you absolutely must watch, read or listen to today: The AJC’s Daniel Flick went deep on the Falcons’ decision to start Tua Tagovailoa in Week 1 and what it means for Atlanta . It’s not a popular opinion, but I tend to agree with the AJC’s Ken Sugiura, who says the cautious approach with Michael Penix Jr. is the right one . The Athletic’s latest NFL power rankings by Josh Kendall and Chad Graff have the Falcons ranked 26th. Do you agree? Also from The Athletic: This was a really interesting read from Austin Mock on his new QB ranking metric, QB Index . Using this methodology, Mock ranked Kirk Cousins 24th last year, while Michael Penix Jr. ranked 33rd, and Tua ranked 35th. I’m curious what y’all think of this one. If you want to chat about tonight’s Super Bowl rematch between the Patriots and Seahawks with other NFL fans, check out SB Nation’s NFL Feed ! From the Falcoholic Community Speaking of Gervon Dexter … this man is an ATHLETE. This is a great find and share from iNFiNiTE GHOST. The Falcoholic’s Question of the Day: Looking at the Falcons’ schedule, I could see them pulling Tua and starting Michael Penix Jr. for the first time after Thursday Night Football against the Packers in Week 4. So I’ll go on record saying I believe Tua will start four games, with Penix making his triumphant (hopefully!) return in New Orleans on Monday Night Football against the Saints in Week 5. What do you think? How many games will Tua start for Atlanta this season, and why? Tell us in the comments.

title: Falcons depth chart: Rookies Kendal Daniels, Avieon Terrell listed as starters for Week 1
summary: The release of the depth chart in a given week is only noteworthy when it contains new information that was not previously known to us, and that doesn’t happen all that often. For Week 1, most of the depth chart drama figured to be out of the way with the announcement that Tua Tagovailoa is […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Atlanta linebacker Kendal Daniels (53) reacts during the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The release of the depth chart in a given week is only noteworthy when it contains new information that was not previously known to us, and that doesn’t happen all that often. For Week 1, most of the depth chart drama figured to be out of the way with the announcement that Tua Tagovailoa is the starting quarterback to start the season. Not all of it, though. We had not yet had it confirmed that rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels would be starting next to Divine Deablo, a post-draft prediction of mine that looked good all summer but was not yet official. We also didn’t know who the starting nickel cornerback would be, though Darnay Holmes ending up on the practice squad and Billy Bowman not being quite ready to get back on the field pointed toward rookie Avieon Terrell. Today, both of those are official (or as official as it gets for an “unofficial” depth chart). I had high hopes for both rookies, and it’s particularly impressive for Terrell to grab this opportunity given that team observers felt Darnay Holmes was in the driver’s seat. The Falcons will have to figure out how to work Bowman in once he returns, but Terrell’s ball hawking abilities, coverage skills, and comfort at nickel made him a logical choice for the nickel spot in the here and now. Long-term I do think we may see him start next opposite his brother A.J. outside, but the trio of two Terrells and Mike Hughes will all be out there in Week 1 regardless. No matter where he winds up lining up this season, Avieon should be a starter the whole way. So should Daniels, if all goes well. Drafted in the fourth round, Daniels immediately looked like a Jeff Ulbrich favorite in the making giving his length, physicality, and coverage ability, which led me to believe he’d be very much in the mix for a starting job. The Falcons now have talented young depth behind him with Christian Harris (who he outdueled for the starting job) and rookie Harold Perkins Jr., plus veteran Josh Woods, but I’m willing to bet Daniels will fare well minus some inevitable rookie hiccups. He was extremely impressive in training camp and preseason. The other interesting note from this depth chart? While it’s little surprise that Zachariah Branch is listed as the team’s punt returner, Brian Robinson Jr. being the kick returner was not set in stone. If Tyler Goodson is flexed to the active roster, I’ll be interested to see if he gets a look there, but it’s worth noting that Robinson averaged nearly 30 yards per return in 2025 with the 49ers. Atlanta’s often moribund return game should get a boost from him and Branch. Congratulations to both rookies, and I’m excited to see them out there against the Steelers.
author: Dave Choate

title: Breaking down what the decision to start Tua Tagovailoa means for the Falcons and players involved
summary: The Atlanta Falcons finally made it official yesterday, declaring Tua Tagovailoa the starter for Week 1 of the 2026 season. The quarterback controversy and competition has been settled, but not definitively and not for the long haul, and therein lies the rub. The Falcons went out this spring and signed Tua as both competition and […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Atlanta quarterbacks Tua Tagovailoa (1) and Michael Penix Jr. (9) ask for the game ball after quarterback Jack Strand (18) (not pictured) scored a touchdown during the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons finally made it official yesterday, declaring Tua Tagovailoa the starter for Week 1 of the 2026 season. The quarterback controversy and competition has been settled, but not definitively and not for the long haul, and therein lies the rub. The Falcons went out this spring and signed Tua as both competition and insurance for Michael Penix Jr., who told media (and the team, obviously) that he was close but not quite ready to play. It seems fairly evident that the Falcons wanted to start Penix, whose contract situation, youth, and arm give him a much better chance to be the team’s long-term option, but were thwarted by the reality that Penix is not ready to go. That makes this announcement one that carries an asterisk, albeit one Tua can erase himself by playing high-end football. What does this all mean for the Falcons right now? What might it mean in the future? Let’s meander together through the thorny thicket that is this quarterback situation. This is a golden opportunity for Tua Let’s be blunt: A totally healthy Penix likely outduels Tua for this starting job, even if he’s not lights out. The Falcons have Penix under contract next year already and have a fifth-year option on his deal they can exercise in April for the 2028 season, giving them plenty of incentive to see how Penix fares in this Kevin Stefanski/Tommy Rees offense before 2026 is up. Tua also had a mediocre sort of summer, showing his appealing accuracy and a solid command of the offense at times and fumbling multiple times in preseason games and looking overmatched at other times. Penix could have beaten him out for this job. But he didn’t, and while Tua’s leash is likely to be short, the veteran quarterback can solve that little problem by playing well when the lights come on. With multiple concussions, a recent history of struggles, and a skill set that teams don’t value particularly highly (smallish, accurate but not strong-armed, doesn’t add much as a runner), Tua desperately needs to impress this year to earn his next contract as a starter and avoid settling fully into his Andy Dalton career arc. Even if the Falcons want to find a pretext to play Penix at some point, if Tua can log a half a season or more looking like the Tua of old, he’ll get a short-term starting contract from the Falcons or someone else. Likely someone else, but still. The reason this opportunity is so appealing is that the Falcons have a lot of talent for Tua to work with. Drake London is a big, sure-handed target who can be a factor anywhere he lines up, Kyle Pitts already has a stellar rapport with Tua, and Jahan Dotson and Zachariah Branch offer you intriguing speed to turn screens and short passes into major gains. Bijan Robinson, meanwhile, is a tremendous checkdown option who can do damage of his own on screens and lining up as a receiver. Pair that with a solid offensive line and Tua is equipped with the tools he needs to thrive, especially since Rees is going to look to tailor this passing game to accommodate his accuracy and limitations. There’s a major difference in earnings between that contract and signing on to be, say, the backup for the Bengals, and I genuinely do not think Tua will get another real look at a clear-cut starting job without a terrific stint in Atlanta. It’s all in front of him—and the Falcons have enough playmakers for him to work with—but it’s incumbent on the quarterback to make the most of a chance. That’s especially important because… Michael Penix Jr. will be ready soon, and has a narrow path to become Atlanta’s franchise quarterback I don’t think Penix will drag this out, because his career depends on A) playing well and B) playing at all. Penix saying he’s not 100% has already earned him withering criticism on social media from some fans and analysts who perceive him to be dodging an opportunity to start; I don’t personally share that opinion about a guy who has had several major injuries and knows what it takes to return from them. I would humbly suggest that the reputation one can earn from not rushing back from injury and being open and transparent about not wanting to do that can hurt an NFL player’s career, whether that’s fair or not, and if he’s not ready to go and Tua struggles out of the gate things are going to get awfully ugly awfully quickly in terms of how Penix is perceived. But I think given that Penix was medically cleared and says he’s close, it’s safe to assume he’ll be ready to go by the end of the first month of the season. Because he was not ready to go at the beginning of the season and is prioritizing his health, he now has to wait for Tua Tagovailoa to falter to get his shot. Because he was not ready to go at the beginning of the season and because his health is a question mark over the long haul, the Falcons will be hesitant to commit to him past this year if he’s not both injury-free and excellent when he does get into the lineup. Functionally, this means Penix both has to wait for Tua to wilt and be ready to go when that happens and play very well and avoid any further major injuries and hope the coaching staff and front office decide he’s the future in Atlanta. All of this was going to be difficult to do if he was the Week 1 starter, but it becomes more difficult now that he has to wait for an opportunity to open back up. If your faith in Tua is zero, of course, maybe you don’t think Penix will have to wait that long. Penix being the guy is the cleanest solution for this team, because it removes the need to pursue a quarterback next year, gives them a reasonably young player with real talent who is under contract next year and has a fifth year option, and unlocks the deep passing game for the Falcons. It’s still the outcome I’m ultimately rooting for, even though I’m hoping that Tua plays well right now because I don’t want this team to be in the toilet before September is over. But it is a narrow path for Penix, who has much to prove and many variables at play that could continue to slow his return to the field, to prove he deserves to be the franchise quarterback for the Atlanta Falcons. Am I hopeful he’ll get there? Yes, for so many reasons. But we have to acknowledge that there are elements both in his control and well outside of it that have to align here in order for Penix to make a big impression in a relatively short time. The Falcons seem likely to choose a new direction in 2027 So, just to recap, since 2022: In 2022, the Falcons traded Matt Ryan, drafted Desmond Ridder, started Marcus Mariota until that went awry, and then gave Ridder an audition In 2023, started Desmond Ridder until the wheels fell off, started Taylor Heinicke, gave the job back to Ridder, trotted out Heinicke, and then were forced to end the season starting Ridder In 2024, signed Kirk Cousins and drafted Michael Penix Jr. and started Cousins until that went poorly, then gave Penix an audition In 2025, started Penix until he got hurt and then rolled out Cousins the rest of the year In 2026, now are starting Tua with Penix waiting for his shot, with both quarterbacks having significant injury history and the team carrying four players on the depth chart The Falcons have had multiple starters and uncertainty at quarterback every single year since they jettisoned Ryan, whether they knew it going into the season or not, and almost certainly will be in a similar boat in 2026. I think this new regime came into 2026 knowing full well that this was a possibility, but now that it’s actually here and Tua’s starting with a short leash and…
author: Dave Choate

title: How the Falcons can start reviving a dejected fanbase with low expectations
summary: Whenever a team finds itself alone in a category except for the New York Jets, it most likely has fallen on hard times. That’s where the Falcons are when it comes to playoff appearances since 2020. After the Panthers won the NFC South last season, only the Falcons and Jets remain as teams that haven’t […]
full_text: (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Whenever a team finds itself alone in a category except for the New York Jets, it most likely has fallen on hard times. That’s where the Falcons are when it comes to playoff appearances since 2020. After the Panthers won the NFC South last season, only the Falcons and Jets remain as teams that haven’t made the playoffs in the 2020s. Considering the state of the NFC South since Tom Brady retired after the 2022 season, it’s unfathomable that the Falcons haven’t won the division. They made significant free agency investments in 2023 and 2024 to put themselves in a position to bring playoff football back to Atlanta. They swept the team that finished in first place in Tampa Bay in 2024. The front office went all in on drafting two highly regarded edge rushers in the first round to address the most significant flaw on the roster last year. None of it has resulted in making a playoff appearance. Three consecutive disappointing years have led to multiple coaching changes, four starting quarterbacks, and exceptional players on both sides of the ball deserving so much better. It has left a fanbase largely jaded. From the Arthur Smith-Desmond Ridder debacle in 2023 to Kirk Cousins collapsing in 2024 to Raheem Morris losing control last year, the consistent failure has been heavy for a franchise that can’t figure things out. Matt Ryan becoming the Falcons’ President of Football provided a much-needed spark. It will take much more than the return of a franchise legend to inject optimism into a franchise that hasn’t made the playoffs since Nick Foles’ peak. New coach Kevin Stefanski needs to build a true identity. Ian Cunningham must prove his promising start as general manager leads to lasting success. That starts with young players emerging on one of the league’s oldest rosters. Whether the Falcons make the playoffs or not won’t determine their success in 2026. Several personnel concerns exist across the roster, none bigger than at the sport’s most important position. Putting playoff expectations on a team that doesn’t know which quarterback will start the most games for them isn’t practical. That shouldn’t prevent them from making strides as a franchise. The revamped coaching staff and promising talent are there for genuine growth in Atlanta. Overcoming quarterback uncertainty through coaching Other than Kevin O’Connell, it’s hard to find a current head coach who has endured more quarterback instability yet still found ways to succeed than Stefanski. You lose count trying to remember all the different signal callers he had to work with for six seasons in Cleveland. That’s a challenge the two-time Coach of the Year will have to take on again in 2026. The difference is he has a more solidified offensive infrastructure with legitimate firepower. A trio of Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts creates exciting possibilities no matter who is under center. An offensive line returning four starters, with Bill Callahan coaching them, provides stability that was lost in his final years in Cleveland. The pieces are there to construct an efficient offense that can outscore teams, even with the glaring quarterback limitations. Diversifying the run game will be crucial in controlling tempo and wearing down opposing fronts. After relying too heavily on outside zone for multiple seasons, adding more gap-scheme concepts should bring more consistency on the ground. Increasing play-action usage and more varied formations are other potential schematic assets that Stefanski brings to the table. The overall offense needed a total reset after it became so predictable under Zac Robinson. Questions linger about the game plan, whether it’s for Tua Tagovailoa early in the year and perhaps Michael Penix Jr. later on. There’s also skepticism about Tommy Rees as offensive coordinator, as Cleveland ranked 30th in EPA per play when he took over play-calling duties in Week 10 last season. While the Falcons’ offense is significantly more talented, can Rees work with Stefanski to help maximize the quarterback’s capabilities? Whether it’s a quick-pass, heavy RPO system with Tagovailoa or a more aggressive shotgun-based plan with Penix Jr., the Falcons invested too much into their offense to be below average. Stefanski worked wonders with Cleveland in 2020 and 2023 when expectations weren’t exactly high. Some of it came from utilizing heavier personnel packages, running 12 and 13 looks, creating more high-percentage looks in the passing game, and putting the offense in better down-and-distances. Attacking defenses with a wide variety of screens was another key component to his success. These are ideal strategies the Falcons can use, given where they stand at quarterback and wide receiver. That said, Stefanski must be decisive, alongside Rees, to execute his vision with the right quarterback on the current roster. Based on how much Tagovailoa has struggled this summer, Penix Jr. appears to be his best option, but Penix is not ready to start just yet. Staying afloat defensively while a stellar secondary establishes itself Jeff Ulbrich deserves enormous praise for the defense’s elevation last season. After his return to Atlanta initially underwhelmed many people, he silenced critics with his pressure plans and coverage variation. The franchise record for most sacks in a season was broken without a game-changing edge rusher on the roster, with defensive line coach Nate Ollie also deserving major credit. While James Pearce Jr. broke the franchise record for most sacks by a rookie in a season, he didn’t take over games. It took a cohesive effort for them to overwhelm some of the league’s best offenses in dramatic upset victories. Many of the players who were at the forefront of their success aren’t with the team going into the season. According to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution’s Daniel Flick, only 28.1% of the sack production will be on the opening-day roster. That total will increase when Pearce Jr. returns from suspension in Week 9. That won’t change the fact that this is a major obstacle for Ulbrich to overcome. Losing Jalon Walker for the season was a devastating blow after his promising rookie season. While it’s encouraging that the new regime was proactive in signing ZaDarius Smith and trading for Gervon Dexter Sr. to add talent up front, it’s difficult to envision the front imposing their will on many offensive lines. That not only increases the pressure on Ulbrich to call more twists and blitzes. It raises expectations for an ultra-talented secondary to lead the overall unit. Expectations must be high when a group features an All-Pro safety, Pro Bowl-caliber cornerback, an emerging ball-hawking safety, and two promising cornerbacks, as well as a well-regarded secondary coach in Justin Hood. It likely won’t happen on opening day, but Jessie Bates, A.J. Terrell, Xavier Watts, Avieon Terrell, and Billy Bowman Jr. should be on the field together at some point. Assembling those five players should fluster quarterbacks and produce turnovers. I wrote about how special the secondary can be a month ago. While Mike Hughes will start the season, things could change as Avieon Terrell proves he can handle playing significant snaps and Bowman Jr. is healthy. Bates and Watts are consistently around the ball, attempting to make game-changing plays. A.J. Terrell is quietly coming off one of his better years. This group has all the pieces to take a significant leap to become one of the league’s best. Along with Divine Deablo, it’s the best hope to keep the defense stabilized after enduring significant losses. Brandon Dorlus’ rapid ascendance, with Maason Smith and Dexter Sr. becoming dependable, will be pivotal. The possibility of Kendal Daniels or Harold Perkins Jr. emerging as a three-down linebacker creates more long-term progression for a unit that will feel the loss of Kaden Elliss in a multitude of…

title: 5 bold predictions for the Ravens 2026 season
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are set to kick off their 2026 season this coming Sunday, with a trip to Indianapolis for a showdown with the Colts. After a long offseason and summer period, a much-anticipated season is now within days of commencing. Many predictions and projections have been made about what will transpire for the Ravens […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - DECEMBER 14: Kyle Hamilton #14 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on during the first quarter of the NFL 2025 game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on December 14, 2025 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are set to kick off their 2026 season this coming Sunday, with a trip to Indianapolis for a showdown with the Colts. After a long offseason and summer period, a much-anticipated season is now within days of commencing. Many predictions and projections have been made about what will transpire for the Ravens this coming season, a lot of which are realistic. Let’s go a bit further and run through some bolder predictions that, while maybe less realistic, are still possible. Here are five bold predictions for the Ravens in 2026. Jovaughn Gwyn starts all 17 games and gets a contract extension The starting center competition was finally settled earlier this week, at least for now, when head coach Jesse Minter named Gwyn the team’s starter. Minter was clear that this was a decision for Week 1 and Ethan Pocic is still working his way back into form from injury, which suggests Gwyn’s leash as the starter will be short. This is plenty fair given the 27-year-old has never started an NFL game, whereas Pocic is much more proven and experienced. However, Gwyn has shown a lot of promise in training camp and the preseason. He possesses good athletic traits and is a seamless scheme fit with offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, whom he spent time with in Atlanta. The Ravens signed Gwyn shortly after hiring Ledford. Can Gwyn fully fill the shoes of Tyler Linderbaum as a perennial Pro Bowler? Most likely not, but the stage is set for him to play well enough to maintain a grip on the starting job for the full season. To go a step a further, if he performs adequately, the Ravens could pursue signing him to an affordable multi-year contract extension, ensuring continuity at the position and eliminating the need to find another starter again next year. Matthew Hibner leads the tight end room in receiving yards The Ravens have high hopes for each of their rookie tight ends to contribute right away. Frankly, they need at least one of Hibner or Josh Cuevas to develop into at least a complimentary receiving role to help fill the absences of Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar. Between the two, Hibner projects to be a more likely instant producer given his athletic profile and yards-after-catch ability. While Mark Andrews has long been the team’s leading receiver at the position, the veteran has seen a decline in production and athleticism in recent years. 2025 was Andrews’ least productive statistical season since his rookie campaign. He can still be of value to the Ravens’ offense as a security blanket and chain-mover on third downs, but incorporating Hibner in a larger capacity as the season progresses makes sense. Andrews averaged only 24.8 receiving yards per game last year. Hibner has the upside to receive a handful of catches per game if he develops in the offensive attack, and the downfield yards-after-catch skills to turn his receptions into solid yardage. Nate Wiggins makes an All-Pro team After quickly developing into a surefire starter in his rookie season, Wiggins’ 2025 campaign was more up and down than many anticipated. Wiggins allowed almost 800 receiving yards but was targeted more than any other cornerback (112 times) and was in a defensive ecosystem that was in-flux many times, particularly in the secondary. Under Minter and new specialization coaches, Wiggins is in position to have a standout season. The 23-year-old is the team’s best coverage corner and thrives as a sticky press man defender. His athletic traits and ball skills have been on display frequently during his two career seasons, it’s just a matter of playing more consistently and putting it all together. Many other cornerbacks in recent years have made a jump to stardom in the middle of their rookie contract, such as Christian Gonzalez and Devon Witherspoon. Wiggins may not instantly become one of the few best corners in the league, but if he’s a starring presence on one of the top defensive units in the league this coming season, All-Pro recognition is within reach. Kyle Hamilton wins Defensive Player of the Year The last time a safety won the Defensive Player of the Year (DPOY) award was in 2010, when Troy Polamalu earned the trophy for the Pittsburgh Steelers. Before that, it was Ravens’ legend Ed Reed in 2004, and only two other instances ever since the award commenced. So, it’s very rare for a safety to win DPOY, but Kyle Hamilton is also rare talent who’s capable of breaking the norm. Hamilton’s reputation precedes him now through four career seasons, as a perennial All-Pro and widely recognized as the top overall safety in the league. Even so, it’s still plenty possible that there are heights he’s yet to reach as a player. Hamilton is primed to thrive in Minter’s defensive scheme, where defensive backs are put in the best position to succeed and maximize their talents. Minter got the best out of veteran Derwin James, who is similar to Hamilton in terms of versatility and skill set, but the latter is younger and more in his prime. In order to actually win the DPOY award, Hamilton would need to rack up notable counting stats like forced turnovers and sacks, while coming up with highlight-reel plays in big moments. If he does this and is again the defensive leader for a top-ranked defensive unit, and hopefully one of the league’s best teams, Hamilton’s national recognition could apex to another level. Jesse Minter wins Coach of the Year The Coach of the Year (COTY) award is often a narrative-driven award, where the winner is the head coach of a team that fits one or more of the following criteria: exceeded expectations in a big way, experienced a significant turnaround from the season prior, or finished atop or near the top of the NFL standings. If all goes according to plan for the Ravens in 2026, Minter may perfectly fit the bill for all of these. It’s not an extremely bold prediction to say Minter will win COTY, given he’s one of the betting favorites. However, given the unpredictable nature of NFL season year-to-year, there’s no telling what unforeseen coaches can emerge as COTY candidates. Minter profiles as a real potential winner given the Ravens underwhelmed and missed the playoffs last season, setting the stage for a turnaround season where the head coach is a leading factor. If the Ravens have an elite defense, in particular, that will bode well for Minter’s chances as well. Perhaps the final piece of the puzzle would be just how good the Ravens are in the regular season. If they can win the division and have one of the best records in the conference, which are achievable feats, Minter’s case to be named Coach of the Year will only become stronger. 5

title: Dark horse Jovaughn Gwyn wins Ravens’ Week 1 starting center job
summary: Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter announced that Jovaughn Gwyn would start at center for the 2026 regular-season opener against the Indianapolis Colts. “ I would say that’s a Week 1 decision — not necessarily a permanent decision,” Minter added, noting that former Browns starter Ethan Pocic was “still coming back” from a torn Achilles […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - AUGUST 22: Baltimore Ravens guard Jovaughn Gwyn (54) warms up before the NFL preseason game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Minnesota Vikings on August 22nd, 2026, at U.S. Bank in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter announced that Jovaughn Gwyn would start at center for the 2026 regular-season opener against the Indianapolis Colts. “ I would say that’s a Week 1 decision — not necessarily a permanent decision,” Minter added, noting that former Browns starter Ethan Pocic was “still coming back” from a torn Achilles suffered last December. Gwyn, 27, will now make his first career start against the Colts’ ferocious defensive tackle duo of DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart. This will be an early test for offensive coordinator Declan Doyle’s new scheme and quarterback Lamar Jackson’s command of it at the line of scrimmage. The Ravens’ starting center competition was one of the team’s biggest offseason storylines following Tyler Linderbaum’s departure in free agency. Gwyn was seen as a dark horse after spending three years in Atlanta with offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford, who had a loud voice in The Castle this offseason. Former Colts backup Danny Pinter seemed to take an early lead in spring practices, and Pocic’s arrival in July threatened to push Gwyn to the third string once he was healthy. But Gwyn’s standout performance in the Ravens’ first preseason game against the Eagles and Pinter’s season-ending knee injury during joint practices in Minnesota propelled him into the first team. Pocic still got plenty of playing time across the last two preseason games, but he never did enough to displace Gwyn. Minter’s comments also indicate that Pocic is not back at 100% and could factor into the picture later in the season. Gwyn could preempt that with a strong start to the year, especially against such stiff competition. Beyond blocking Buckner and Stewart, he will have to cover all of the mental aspects of the center position. His ability to read the defense and communicate the calls in partnership with Jackson at the line of scrimmage will be crucial. The Ravens’ decision is another sign of Ledford’s influence within the organization. The team declined to trade up for a center on Day 2 or select one of the several Power Four starters who were available on Day 3, instead trusting their new offensive line coach to coach up one of their other options. Among them was Gwyn, a 2023 seventh-round pick out of South Carolina who Ledford developed in Atlanta and brought with him to Baltimore this offseason. Gwyn stayed on the Falcons’ practice squad for two years before earning the backup center job in 2025. Early struggles from Gwyn would be a significant problem for the Ravens offense. They would also offer a glimpse at Minter’s in-season management style. Would he be quick to replace Gwyn with Pocic, or would he fall into the past regime’s frustrating pattern of leaving subpar blockers on the field for far too long? The new head coach has preached standards and accountability since he arrived in Baltimore; that would be a chance to practice them. The Ravens, of course, will be hoping that situation never comes up. It is worth noting that Gwyn is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent this offseason – as is Pocic – so Minter’s mention of a non-permanent decision also (perhaps inadvertently) references the team’s lack of a long-term at the center position. But for at least one week, it will be Gwyn snapping the ball to Jackson when the Ravens offense takes the field.
