title: Week 1 rooting interests for Buffalo Bills fans
summary: We made it, Bills Mafia.   The NFL season kicks off tonight. We have hours and hours of meaningful football ahead of us this weekend, and we definitely aren’t going to watch it without choosing sides. We’re the number one fan base in the league, after all.  There’s just one problem: We don’t really know who all of our enemies are yet. We […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: A Buffalo Bills fan holds a sign reading "Bills Mafia" during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bills defeated the Jets 35-8. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images We made it, Bills Mafia. The NFL season kicks off tonight. We have hours and hours of meaningful football ahead of us this weekend, and we definitely aren’t going to watch it without choosing sides. We’re the number one fan base in the league, after all. There’s just one problem: We don’t really know who all of our enemies are yet. We know we will almost never root for the AFC East, but beyond that, there are no playoff scenarios to calculate, no strength-of-victory tiebreakers to chase, and no late-season games where we suddenly find ourselves cheering for a team we’ve spent the previous four months making fun of. Rooting Interests is almost ridiculous in Week 1, but we’re Bills fans, so of course we’re doing it anyway. We don’t know which AFC teams will be standing between Buffalo and the Number 1 seed in January. We don’t know which teams will be fighting for the final wild-card spots, which supposedly good teams will fall apart, or which team nobody is thinking about right now will become a problem. But we still need somebody to root for; so, until the 2026 season gives us enough information to know exactly what Buffalo needs, we’re going to make our own rules. Think of this as the early-season Rooting Interests constitution: Always root for the Bills Build Buffalo’s tiebreakers for later. Knock last year’s AFC division winners down a peg. Push struggling AFC teams away from premium draft picks. Keep the best draft picks in the NFC. When two irrelevant NFC teams play, root for the better team to win and the worse team to lose. When the rules conflict, Buffalo’s 2026 interests come first. And, above all else, never forget that the Patriots, Dolphins and Jets can lose every single game they play, and we won’t feel even a little bit bad about it. One important reminder before we get started: These are rooting interests, not predictions. We aren’t picking who we think will win, who Vegas favors or even necessarily who we think is the better team. We’re simply deciding which outcome Bills Mafia should want based on what could help Buffalo — now, later or somewhere way down the road. AFC East Buffalo Bills over Houston Texans Seattle Seahawks over New England Patriots Tennessee Titans over New York Jets Las Vegas Raiders over Miami Dolphins Rest of the AFC Cincinnati Bengals over Tampa Bay Buccaneers Batlimore Ravens over Indianapolis Colts Cleveland Browns over Jacksonville Jaguars Atlanta Falcons over Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers over Arizona Cardinals Kansas City over Denver Broncos NFC vs NFC games LA Rams over San Francisco 49ers Chicago Bears over Carolina Panthers Detroit Lions over New Orleans Saints Green Bay Packers over Minnesota Vikings* Philadelphia Eagles over Washington Commanders Dallas Cowboys over New York Giants * This one doesn’t really matter. Buffalo plays them both. They had a half game separating them in last year’s final standings. But I’m petty, and the Vikings made me mad, so I’m going Green Bay. Are we going to look back at some of these picks in October and wonder what we were thinking? Almost certainly. There’s a decent chance one of the teams we’re rooting for this week becomes the team we need to lose games in December. But that’s a problem for future Bills Mafia. Right now, we have a full slate of football, a handful of rules, and absolutely no intention of sitting through any of these games without knowing who we want to win. Soon enough, we’ll be digging through strength of victory, conference records, and playoff scenarios looking for every tiny advantage Buffalo can get. The rules will change. The priorities will shift. And the standings will eventually tell us who the real enemies are. The math will come later. For now, we pick sides.

title: Josh Allen series history vs. Houston Texans
summary: The Buffalo Bills will open the 2026 season Sunday at Reliant Stadium against the Houston Texans. It’s a new season, a new coaching staff, a new roster, and a clean record.  There are some places where Josh Allen has built a highlight reel. Houston isn’t one of them.  But there is some history waiting for Allen when he walks back into […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 20: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills reacts as he's sacked during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills will open the 2026 season Sunday at Reliant Stadium against the Houston Texans. It’s a new season, a new coaching staff, a new roster, and a clean record. There are some places where Josh Allen has built a highlight reel. Houston isn’t one of them. But there is some history waiting for Allen when he walks back into that building. Josh Allen has never won in Houston. So, before he gets another shot Sunday, we’re opening the time capsule on Allen’s history with the Texans. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2018: The first trip Allen was a rookie when he made his first trip to Houston on Oct. 14, 2018, and he didn’t finish the game. 22-year-old Allen completed 10 of 17 passes for just 84 yards as Houston’s defense kept pressure on the rookie quarterback. Late in the third quarter, Allen injured his throwing elbow, and Nathan Peterman took over. For a minute, it looked like Buffalo might get out of Houston with the win anyway. Peterman threw a touchdown pass to Zay Jones that gave Buffalo a fourth-quarter lead. But, with the game tied at 13 and less than two minutes remaining, Peterman threw a pick-six. Houston won, 20-13. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2021: The one Buffalo got It would be three years before Allen would see Houston in the regular season again. This time, the Texans came to Buffalo. And this one wasn’t close. Allen completed 20 of 30 passes for 248 yards and two touchdowns as the Bills rolled to a 40-0 win. He also added 41 yards on the ground. It’s Allen’s only victory over Houston. And it happened in Buffalo. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2024: The one everybody circled It would be another three seasons before the Bills and Texans met again. Allen wasn’t a rookie quarterback trying to establish himself in the NFL anymore, he was a household name. But going into that game, he wasn’t the only reason everyone was watching. Stefon Diggs was waiting in Houston. Buffalo had traded Diggs to the Texans during the offseason, setting up a reunion that became a storyline as soon as the schedule was released. Diggs against Buffalo. Allen against Diggs. All the questions about their relationship, the breakup, and what had gone wrong in Buffalo followed both of them into NRG Stadium. Diggs caught six passes for 82 yards. Allen had one of the roughest statistical afternoons of his career. He completed just 9 of 30 passes for 131 yards for a career-low 30% completion rate. Houston took away the deep ball almost completely, with Allen connecting on just one of 15 attempts when he threw the ball at least 10 yards downfield. Still, Buffalo fought back. Houston had led 20-3. The Bills erased all 17 points of that deficit and tied the game in the fourth quarter. Then Houston won. Ka’imi Fairbairn connected from 59 yards as time expired. Texans 23. Bills 20. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2025: The one without a sideshow A year later, Buffalo went back. Diggs was gone. So was the emotional sideshow that had surrounded the matchup a year earlier. Houston didn’t even have its starting quarterback. C.J. Stroud was sidelined, leaving Davis Mills to make the start. This time, Allen’s passing numbers were considerably better. He completed 24 of 34 passes for 253 yards. James Cook ran for 116 yards, including a 45-yard touchdown, and Khalil Shakir caught eight passes for 110 yards. Buffalo outgained Houston 326-261. The Bills ran 10 more offensive plays and held the ball for 32:22 compared with Houston’s 27:38. But those weren’t the numbers that decided the game. Houston sacked Allen eight times. Calen Bullock intercepted him twice and forced a fumble. Buffalo turned the ball over three times. Houston didn’t turn it over once. A year earlier, Diggs had been the story. This time, Diggs was gone. The emotional sideshow was gone. The result wasn’t. Texans 23. Bills 19. _____________________________________________________________________________ Four regular-season games against Houston. Three losses. One win. And that one came in Buffalo. But there’s a fifth game that belongs in our time capsule. Technically, it doesn’t show up when we look at Allen’s regular-season history against the Texans, but Bills Mafia remembers it well. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2019: The one that ended a season Allen’s second trip to Houston wasn’t during the regular season. It was his first NFL playoff game. The Bills arrived at NRG Stadium on Jan. 4, 2020, for an AFC Wild Card matchup, and for much of the game, it looked like Allen’s first playoff start was going to become his first playoff win. Buffalo led 13-0 at halftime. The Bills added another three in the third quarter. Allen had even caught a touchdown pass. Then Houston came back. The Texans erased the 16-point deficit and took a 19-16 lead before Buffalo forced overtime with a field goal in the final seconds of regulation. Allen finished with 264 passing yards and another 92 on the ground. There were flashes of the quarterback Allen was becoming. There were also moments that looked very much like a 23-year-old playing his first postseason game. Allen completed just over 52% of his passes, took three sacks, and finished with a 69.5 passer rating. In the end, it was Deshaun Watson, not Josh Allen, who led the game-winning drive in overtime. Texans 22. Bills 19. _____________________________________________________________________________ So here we are again. Another season. Another trip to Houston. The circumstances have changed drastically since a 22-year-old Allen walked into that stadium for the first time eight years ago. He’s been an MVP. He’s won division titles and playoff games. He’s become franchise quarterback Buffalo needed him to be. But there is still one thing he hasn’t done. Josh Allen has never walked out of Houston with a win. Sunday gives him another chance.

title: Buffalo Bills first depth chart ahead of Week 1 at Houston Texans
summary: The Buffalo Bills have officially entered game-prep ahead of their season-opening trip south to face the Houston Texans. Longtime members of Bills Mafia need few reminders about the house of horrors that is NRG Stadium for Buffalo. Time and again, in spite of those surrounding quarterback Josh Allen and company, the Bills just can’t escape […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 7: Maxwell Hairston #31 of the Buffalo Bills walks onto the field before a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Highmark Stadium on December 7, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have officially entered game-prep ahead of their season-opening trip south to face the Houston Texans. Longtime members of Bills Mafia need few reminders about the house of horrors that is NRG Stadium for Buffalo. Time and again, in spite of those surrounding quarterback Josh Allen and company, the Bills just can’t escape Houston with a win. For a team that hasn’t claimed victory in H-Town since 2006, it’s natural to spend a little extra time glancing over the depth chart. Though it’s the first week and we have yet to receive an official injury report, there are a few things to glean from the Bills’ first unofficial depth chart of the 2026 NFL season . Let’s dive in for a quick look beyond the obvious names and assignments, while remembering that aspects of this list could change before Sunday’s game. Many have wondered how the pecking order would shake out at wide receiver, but there are perhaps few surprises if you’ve been monitoring the situation. Behind obvious starters in DJ Moore and Khalil Shakir, we find that Keon Coleman sitting in the first chair as WR3. Backing up Coleman will be Joshua Palmer, while backing up Moore is rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell. The team doesn’t list anyone behind Shakir, but you can expect Bell and/or Palmer to fill in on an as-needed basis. At running back, it’s Ray Davis in the RB2 spot and ahead of Ty Johnson. Davis is in line for a healthy dose of work this season, given his work on special teams. He’ll of course reprise his role as the team’s primary kick returner (with Ty Johnson listed behind him there, too), and he’s listed as the second punt returner in the teams equation. We still don’t know the status of Johnson following an injury he sustained during the Return of the Blue & Red game. How and if he’s able to contribute could further shape any immediate roster gymnastics. It’s that punt return situation that’s has a lot of people curious. Presently, nickel cornerback Dee Alford is listed as the team’s top punt returner. Keep in mind that Buffalo signed wide receiver Greg Dortch at roster cutdowns, and that once acclimated, he could be elevated to the active roster to carry the load at punt returner. Alford’s main assignment is on defense as the starting nickel cornerback (and immediate backup to Christian Benford), so the situation at punt returner bears watching. Of note to those with a Bills jersey: Cornerback Maxwell Hairston has apparently changed his number, now going with “1” instead of “31” this season. Also, Hairston is listed at starting CB2 over rookie Davison Igbinosun. Elsewhere on defense, we find DeWayne Carter, Greg Gaines, and Landon Jackson as the backups to Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, and T.J. Sanders, respectively. That’s not a huge bit of news, perhaps beyond who was going to claim that third starting defensive line role after Oliver and Walker. At inside linebacker, it’s Dorian Williams over rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr (his direct backup). Joe Andreessen will begin the season as Terrel Bernard’s main backup at linebacker. Bills first unofficial depth chart is out. Among the highlights: It appears Maxwell Hairston has changed his jersey to No. 1. He was No. 31. title: Bills Mafia’s Houston takeover: Where to party before Bills-Texans
summary: The Buffalo Bills open the 2026 regular season against the Houston Texans on Sunday, September 13. But for Bills Mafia traveling to Houston, kickoff is only one part of the weekend. The Houston Bills Backers have two days of festivities planned, beginning with their annual block party at Christian’s Tailgate on Saturday. On Sunday morning, […]
full_text: Bills mafia takes the show on the road, bringing all the tailgate traditions and Bills Backers atmosphere to away cities throughout the season. The Buffalo Bills open the 2026 regular season against the Houston Texans on Sunday, September 13. But for Bills Mafia traveling to Houston, kickoff is only one part of the weekend. The Houston Bills Backers have two days of festivities planned, beginning with their annual block party at Christian’s Tailgate on Saturday. On Sunday morning, fans can choose between the Backers’ traditional tailgate or an all-inclusive option from Fans of Buffalo. Here is what you need to know before the Mafia takes over Houston. Saturday: Bills Block Party at Christian’s Tailgate The weekend begins Saturday, September 12, at Christian’s Tailgate Bar & Grill, the official home of the Houston Bills Backers. Located at 2000 Bagby Street in Midtown Houston, Christian’s will host what it calls the “Best Bills Backer Party in the Country.” The party will include a live DJ, music throughout the day, a mechanical bull, photo opportunities, games, Sahlen’s hot dogs, drink specials and more. Whether you live in Houston or are flying in for the season opener, this is the place to meet up with Bills fans before turning the focus to Sunday. You can find additional information and updates through the official Buffalo Bills Block Party event page . Sunday: Houston Bills Backers tailgate For fans who prefer the traditional Bills tailgating experience, the Houston Bills Backers will open their lot at 6:30 a.m. Sunday. Yes, 6:30 a.m. Bills Mafia does not believe in sleeping in on game day. The tailgate will be held at: 8055 North Stadium Drive Houston, TX Admission is $10 per person for those walking into the lot or $40 per vehicle, regardless of how many people are inside. Payment can be made at the entrance using cash, a credit card, Venmo or Cash App. This is a Rockpile-style, BYOB tailgate, so bring your own beverages, cooler and anything else you need for the morning. Burgers, including a vegetarian option, will be available for purchase from The Burger Joint. The lot will also have restrooms, music and plenty of room for Bills Mafia to spread out. Need some last-minute Bills gear? Merchandise pop-ups will also give fans a chance to add a little more red, white and blue before heading into the game. The private lot is not affiliated with NRG Stadium, so fans parking here should not purchase a separate Texans parking pass. The lot is approximately one mile from the stadium, making for a relatively easy walk to the gates after the tailgate. Sunday: Fans of Buffalo Houston ’26 Tailgate Fans looking for an all-inclusive experience can choose the Fans of Buffalo Houston ’26 Tailgate, located directly next to the Houston Bills Backers’ lot. Instead of packing a cooler and bringing your own food, fans can purchase a package that includes food, drinks, music and a ready-made Bills Mafia party. It is the easier option for anyone traveling from out of town who wants to show up and enjoy the morning without having to assemble a full tailgating setup. The party begins at 7:30 a.m. Sunday, giving fans several hours of food, drinks, music and Bills Mafia fun before kickoff. The current ticket price is $65 per person for the non-alcohol | all you can eat pass. The general admission price including all you can eat and an open bar is $95. The food menu includes options such as BBQ chicken, grilled shrimp, pork belly, Buffalo chicken dip, potato salad, fries, fresh fruit and pan dulce. Unlike the Backers’ BYOB option, this package is designed for fans who would rather show up and have the food and drinks handled for them. Space is limited, and passes are expected to sell out, as they do every year. Tickets are available through the official Fans of Buffalo Houston ’26 Tailgate page on TickPick: Fans of Buffalo ‘26 Houston Tailgate The two Sunday tailgates are directly beside one another so make sure you pick the one that is right for you. Whichever option you choose, you will be surrounded by Bills Mafia and within an easy walk of the stadium. Houston is ready for the Mafia Bills fans have never needed much help turning a road game into a home-away-from-home experience, and Houston makes it especially easy. Start at Christian’s Tailgate on Saturday. On Sunday morning, choose between the Houston Bills Backers’ traditional BYOB setup and the all-inclusive Fans of Buffalo experience. Grab some food, browse the merchandise pop-ups, enjoy the music and then make the walk into the stadium with hundreds of fellow Bills fans. And here’s your official reminder…the Bills and Texans kick off at noon Central Time, so arrive early, have your fun… but leave enough time for the walk and stadium entry!

title: Buffalo Bills must be prepared for this unique characteristic of Texans defense
summary: The Houston Texans aren’t an exotic defense. They don’t utilize creativity get to the quarterback on a regular basis. It’s probably the NFL’s most straight-forward, pin-your-ears-back defensive scheme. That is not to say the Bills can scrap the gameplanning portion of this week for what their offense will see across the line of scrimmage on […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 20: James Cook III #4 of the Buffalo Bills runs with the ball and scores a touchdown during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Houston Texans aren’t an exotic defense. They don’t utilize creativity get to the quarterback on a regular basis. It’s probably the NFL’s most straight-forward, pin-your-ears-back defensive scheme. That is not to say the Bills can scrap the gameplanning portion of this week for what their offense will see across the line of scrimmage on a play-to-play basis in Week 1. It’s to suggest their strategy for attacking Houston’s vaunted defense needs to be anchored in not expecting extra rushers being sent toward Josh Allen. Last season, the Texans had the lowest blitz rate in all of football, at just 16.7%, yet finished seventh with a pressure rate of 40.3%, per Fantasy Points Data — a dream scenario for any defensive coordinator. That combination was integral to that unit’s excellence. And Houston was able to essentially duplicate those magical percentages in the game against the Bills in Week 12 last year. In that victory, the Texans blitzed Allen on just 15.2% of his 39 drop backs and still managed to pressure him 43.5% of the time. Seven of his eight sacks came without a blitz! That has to be exceptionally rare in the NFL. And check the difference for Allen in that game, split by when he was blitzed and not blitzed. Josh Allen vs. Texans in 2025 Completions / Attempts Yards (YPA) TD / INT Rating Not Blitzed 19 / 28 186 (6.6) 0 / 2 56.5 Blitzed 5 / 6 67 (11.2) 0 / 0 113.2 Of course, Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins were dinged in that contest. The former toughed it out but clearly was not himself, and Dawkins left the game for a long stretch, which led to 17 relief-appearance snaps for Ryan Van Demark. Dalton Kincaid didn’t play due to that knee injury. There was no Keon Coleman. Also, Allen dropped back to pass on 28 of 39 plays in the second half, an aerial-centric attack I’d normally advocate for, but such telegraphing in that particular game felt far from ideal. The Bills ran 10 plays out of “empty,” which means five blockers and no one in the backfield or attached to the line for chipping help, more than double the NFL’s average of 4.5 empty plays per contest. Heck, Joe Brady even admitted to a less-than-stellar play-calling job after the defeat. But it’s not as though Allen — and Brady — regularly struggled against teams that played coverage against the Bills offense and held back on blitzing. Even with this Week 12 performance included, Allen’s 105.4 quarterback rating against no-blitz plays from opposing defenses ranked third-best in the entire NFL among qualifying passers. His Expected Points Added per drop back ranked 7th out of 38 qualifiers against no blitz last season. If that game is removed, that rating jumped to 110.4, quite naturally. As a longtime Bills pass-game pusher, particularly due to Allen’s presence, it’s somewhat unorthodox for me to advocate for the run game. Then again, it’s not lost on me that James Cook is the league’s reigning rushing champion, and in the first half of that Week 12 outing a season ago, he had 71 yards on seven carries including a 45-yard touchdown run. More Cook in this game — probably a smart idea for the Bills, because he’s clearly one of the league’s most explosive offensive weapons, and his continued usage keeps Houston’s pass rush honest. Limiting the Texans duo of Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter is, of course, vital to beating this AFC South team. Buffalo has preached the “they have to play us” mentality all offseason, and playing the Bills is dealing with Allen, his assembly of pass catchers… and Cook. We’ll see if Brady learned his lesson schematically from last year’s contest. How do you think the Bills should handle the Texans minimal-blitzing defense?

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 4 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 24: Luke Kuechly #59 of the Carolina Panthers reacts during a game against the New Orleans Saints at the Mercedes Benz Superdome on November 24, 2019 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Jonathan Bachman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #4. Luke Kuechly Welcome to football season. Today is the first day of the NFL season, and there are just four days separating us from the start of Panthers football for the 2026 season. It seems fitting that the subject of today’s countdown piece is the Panther that was just enshrined in the Hall of Fame as part of the class of 2026, Luke Kuechly. Luke Kuechly is an all time example of a questionable process resulting in an incredible result. The Panthers drafted Kuechly ninth overall in 2012 despite having a three time Pro Bowler playing at his position (though he was coming off a significant injury, to be fair). They also had Thomas Davis trying to come back from his knee injuries and the evert reliable James Anderson at the other linebacker positions. Linebacker is typically not a premier position in general, so using a top 10 pick on one when you don’t really need one isn’t a great allocation of resources. But the move couldn’t have turned out better. Jon Beason, who never missed a start in his four years in the league, could never stay healthy after his achilles tear in 2011. His season ended after just four games due to a shoulder injury during Kuechly’s rookie season. Kuechly would step in as the starting middle linebacker to begin one of the greatest primes the league has ever seen at that position. Kuechly was on and off the field while Beason was healthy, which resulted in a slow start out of the gates. However, he played every snap from the time Beason was hurt through the end of the season and was able to amass a league high 164 tackles. That earned him Defensive Rookie of the Year Honors. That season would also be the only season of his career in which he wasn’t an All Pro. Luke Kuechly dominated the game from the linebacker spot in a way few players could. He was a maniacal film studier, which allowed him to key in on opposing offenses and diagnose plays even before the ball was snapped. In the run game, he would frequently beat running backs to the hole or shoot gaps right off the snap. He was elite in coverage as well, using his speed and anticipation to cover enormous amounts of ground and undercut routes in the middle of the field. His motor was relentless, and you’d be hard pressed to find many plays in which he wasn’t around the ball by the end of it. Kuechly’s career was cut short by repeated concussions, so he didn’t amass the counting stats that other all time greats have, but there is no denying the greatness of his peak. In his eight seasons, he was a first team All Pro five times and a second team All Pro twice. He led the league in tackles twice and intercepted at least one pass in every season. He finished his career with 21 interceptions (including postseason) and he ran three of those back for touchdowns. Two of those pick sixes came in the 2015 run to the Super Bowl. Kuechly returned to the Panthers a scout after his retirement but resigned from that job after just a year. He later joined the team as a color commentator on radio broadcasts along side Jake Delhomme. He’s now going to be the lead color commentator for NFL games on Netflix, so we’ll get to hear him in action on Thursday. Luke Kuechly was enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame back in August, He’s the second player to spend the majority of their career with the Panthers to make the Hall of Fame, and he’s the first player to be drafted in the 2010s to make the Hall of Fame. It’s hard to earn that honor playing just eight seasons of NFL football, but that shows just how dominant Kuechly was during those eight seasons. There are very few players that played NFL football at a higher level, and for that, Luke Kuechly lands at number 4 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 02: Steve Smith #89 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after a catch during their game against the San Francisco 49ers at Bank of America Stadium on December 2, 2007 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #5. Steve Smith, Sr Throughout the history of sports, there have been many players who play with a chip on their shoulder. This skill of turning extrinsic motivation intrinsic has allowed countless players to go beyond their limits and dominate their opponents. Steve Smith might have had the largest chip ever. Standing at just 5’9” and weighing under 200 pounds, Smith was overlooked by major college programs. He started his collegiate career at Santa Monica College before transferring to Utah for his junior campaign. Smith immediately made an impact, especially on special teams, scoring 11 total touchdowns including an NCAA high three punt return touchdowns. His senior season in 2000 was not as spectacular, but he still averaged over 20 yards per reception. The lack of definitive improvement from his junior season to his senior year led to him dropping down draft boards, which turned out to be incredibly lucky for the Carolina Panthers. In the 2001 NFL Draft, the Panthers took Dan Morgan in the first round, Kris Jenkins in the second, and finally took Smith in the third round. Despite major pundits like The Sporting News declaring that the team wasted a third round pick on a guy who would just be a punt returner, Smith became a dominant force on the offense just as the other two became dominant pieces for Carolina’s defense. The pundits weren’t wrong about Smith’s impact on special teams, either. On his first career touch, Smith took the opening kickoff of the 2001 season against the Minnesota Vikings 93 yards for a touchdown, one of three return touchdowns his rookie year (two kickoff returns, one punt return). Smith ended up being one of the few bright spots in that doomed 2001 season, earning Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro honors as a returner. The 2002 season showed flashes of what would come from the wide receiver Steve Smith. Paired up with Muhsin Muhammad, the duo put up some decent stats despite less than stellar quarterback play. As was the case for most Panthers, it was 2003 that really shone a spotlight on Smith’s talent. He exploded onto the scene with 88 catches for 1,110 yards and seven touchdowns, adding another punt return touchdown for good measure. His impact went beyond the box score, however, as he became new quarterback Jake Delhomme’s favorite target. The unforgettable Super Bowl run was largely driven by a dominant defense, but Smith provided the offensive fireworks necessary for the team to advance. His 32 yard touchdown catch in the third quarter of the Wild Card game against the Dallas Cowboys all but sealed the win for the Panthers, his now infamous 69 yard “X-Clown” touchdown reception in double overtime against the Rams pushed the team into the NFC Championship Game, and he added a game-tying 39 yard touchdown in the second quarter of the Super Bowl. While the Panthers would not see team success of that nature for another dozen years, Smith blossomed into one of the best wide receivers in the NFL. Despite breaking his leg in the first game of the 2004 season, he returned at full strength in 2005, winning the receiving triple crown (though only tied for first in receiving touchdowns). His line of 103 catches for 1.563 yards and 12 touchdowns were video game numbers. Those 103 catches would be Panthers single season records until some guy named Christian McCaffrey came along seven years later, and the 1,563 receiving yards is still a Panthers record. For the second time in his five year career, Smith was named to the Pro Bowl and First Team All Pro roster while also taking home the Comeback Player of the Year Award. He would go on to make three more Pro Bowls (2006, 2008, and 2011) and a Second Team All Pro nod in 2008. With the arrival of new Face of the Franchise Cam Newton, Smith struggled to take on more of a secondary role. While his production was still bordering on elite until 2013, there was always an undercurrent of strife between him and Cam. That sense of locker room distraction combined with the Panthers wanting to get younger and cheaper at the position led to the team releasing Smith in March of 2014. Two days later, he signed with the Baltimore Ravens. He would end up playing three years with the Ravens, even eclipsing the thousand yard mark in 2014. Smith’s contract with the Ravens expired in 2017, and a lack of interest from other teams led to his retirement. Steve Smith’s legacy in Carolina goes well beyond stats, though he holds some incredible receiving marks in Panthers history: he’s the all-time Panthers leader in targets (1,438), catches (836), yards (12,197), touchdowns (67), and yards per game (67). He also leads the team in punt returns (178), punt return yards (1,652), punt return touchdowns (4), and longest punt return (87 yards), while finishing second only to Michael Bates in kickoff returns (98), kickoff return yards (2,371), and kickoff return touchdowns (2). Smith finished his career in the top ten in NFL history in all-purpose yards and should be a Hall of Famer at some point. But it’s not the numbers that matter to Panthers fans, it’s the moments: X-Clown, the 2006 playoff game against the Bears, the sideline quotes, the touchdown celebrations, breaking his arm and still scoring a touchdown against the Giants in 2009, grabbing Malcom Jenkins and dragging him by the facemask after scoring a touchdown against the Saints in 2011, and even (unfortunately) the “blood and guts” game against the Panthers in 2014. Despite all the numbers he racked up on the field, the only number that matters at the end of the day to Panthers fans? 89. Bottom line.

title: 2026 Chicago Bears Season Preview: The Hunter is now the Hunted
summary: For every professional sports team, the end goal is always the same: Win a championship. Although that didn’t happen for the Chicago Bears in 2025, last season was easy to call a dream come true in many ways. Time flies, and sometimes it’s easy to forget the past. For most fans, 2024 was a season […]
full_text: For every professional sports team, the end goal is always the same: Win a championship. Although that didn’t happen for the Chicago Bears in 2025, last season was easy to call a dream come true in many ways. Time flies, and sometimes it’s easy to forget the past. For most fans, 2024 was a season they’d like to purge from their memories forever. While living through former head coach Matt Eberflus’s last season in Chicago wasn’t pleasant, it also reminded everyone to enjoy the good times while they last. That’s exactly what Ben Johnson provided this team last season: Hope. Eberflus became the first head coach in franchise history to be fired midseason. While that alone isn’t uncommon, his failures came at the cost of Caleb Williams’ development as a rookie. Johnson not only righted those wrongs, but he also instilled a new culture in the team and the city that should leave a lasting impression for years to come. Now comes the hard part: Maintaining that success. It’s been 20 years since the Bears experienced back-to-back playoff seasons. Johnson and his team broke multiple “curses” last year. Will this be the next? Despite a lack of “flash” this offseason, the organization is optimistic its core is in place and that last year’s experiences (both good and bad) will give the team more tools to complete the road to Super Bowl 60. With the season set to kick off this week, let’s dive into our yearly Chicago Bears season preview. Offseason Additions Pre-Draft: LB Devin Bush S Coby Bryant C Garrett Bradbury DT Neville Gallimore Others: WR Kalif Raymond, DB Cam Lewis, DT Kentavius Street, DT James Lynch, LB Jack Sanborn, and Xavier Woods. For the first time since the start of the rebuild, general manager Ryan Poles and the team took a more conservative approach to the start of the acquisition period. Losing Drew Dalman to retirement forced a trade for Bradbury, but the primary focus was adding speed. Both Bush and Bryant provide that in the second and third levels of the defense, while Raymond gives Johnson a familiar face to rely on at receiver. Gallimore, Woods, and Lewis should provide quality depth at their respective positions. Oh, and Jack Sanborn is back for a Round 2 with his hometown team. There’s no doubt that this free agency period lacked flash. Now, fans must hope that the core they established last season is enough to take them to the next level in 2026. They’ll be starting the season without Bryant at safety, which is a tough pill to swallow for a team that was hoping he’d set the tone for the entire defense. Draft: Trades: No. 460 to Tennessee Titans for No. 69 and No. 144 No. 129 & No. 144 to Carolina Panthers for No. 124 and No. #166 No. 239 and No. 241 to Buffalo Bills for No. 213 1st Round (#25) S Dillon Thieneman (Oregon) 2nd Round (#57) C Logan Jones (Iowa) 3rd Round (#69) TE Sam Rousch (Stanford) 3rd Round (#89) WR Zavion Thomas (LSU) 4th Round (#124) CB Malik Muhammad (Texas) 5th Round (#166) LB Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State) 6th Round (#213) DT Jordan van den Berg (Georgia Tech) Following a lackluster free agency period, the Bears set their sights on yet another impactful draft class. Thanks to the DJ Moore trade, they came into the draft with four picks over their first three rounds. Round 1 started with a pleasant surprise in Thieneman. It was clear that safety was a top need for them, and having a player projected to go 10 picks early still on the board at 25 was about as good as it gets. They followed up the Thieneman pick with a trio of names on Day 2 that included Jones and two surprises in Roush and Thomas. Not many could have expected them to go all offense on Day 2, especially with the value of some of those picks in question. Luckily, they followed up on Day 3 with a trio of defensive players that, at worst, should provide quality depth over the next few seasons. All in all, this wasn’t the same impactful class as we’ve seen (on paper) over the last few years, but that was expected considering how much lower in each round they picked. All in all, they added what should be multiple Year 1 contributors with the idea of developing them into bigger contributors down the line. Fans shouldn’t expect the same early impact from this class, but as the season goes on, most should settle into roles that have them contributing weekly. Retained Free Agents: LB DeMarco Jackson LT Braxton Jones OL Theo Benedet S Elijah Hicks Others: QB Case Keenum, DE Daniel Hardy, and iOL Jordan McFadden. The ongoing trend of Poles and his front office not retaining many of their impending free agents continued this offseason. Despite having multiple starters hit the market, the team retained just two projected starters, along with some key depth pieces. Jackson was a must-re-sign after a breakout season, and picking up Benedet’s ERFA tag was a no-brainer. Retaining Jones for another year was a mild surprise, but much needed with Ozzy Trapilo’s status for the season still up in the air. The team also decided to keep their quarterback room together for another season, which seems smart after how well things went in 2025. All in all, each move made sense, even if fans expected to see more players back from last year’s roster. Contract Extensions: RT Darnell Wright 4 years, $116 million ($93 million guaranteed) Barring any last-minute surprises, Wright enters the regular season as the only player to receive a long-term extension this offseason. Given the money and resources needed for Caleb Williams and his offensive weapons in the near future, it makes sense. Wright was well-deserving of his new contract, and now holds the highest guarantee of any offensive lineman in NFL history. Offseason Subtractions S Kevin Byard WR DJ Moore (Traded) C Drew Dalman (Retirement) LB Tremaine Edmunds (Released) S Jaquan Brisker DT Gervon Dexter Sr. (Traded) Others: CB Nahshon Wright, WR Olamide Zaccheaus, DB C.J. Gardner-Johnson, DT Andrew Billings, LS Scott Daly, DE Dominique Robinson, LB Amen Ogbongbemiga, iOL Ryan Bates, DE Joe Tryon-Shoyinka, S Jonathan Owens, DT Chris Williams, TE Durham Smythe, CB Nick McCloud, WR Devin Duvernay, RB Travis Homer, and iOL Ricky Stromberg. Heading into the start of the new league year, many expected Byard to be retained on an affordable deal. Despite productive talks heading into the legal negotiation period, the Bears chose a different direction at both safety positions. Moore’s trade surprised some, but for those who watched his usage before Rome Odunze’s injury, it was clear Johnson never valued him as a top option in his offense. Edmunds was a no-brainer to release, considering his play and money owed. Wright and Gardner-Johnson were two unsung heroes of last season’s secondary, but both got bigger deals elsewhere. The rest of the names on this list were simply depth pieces or role players. While it would have been nice to retain more of last year’s “core,” this type of roster churn is expected for every team in the league each offseason. Reasons for Optimism 1. Year 2 of Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams should produce even more fireworks. As expected, last year’s offense looked worlds better than anything we saw under Eberflus. In some ways, it was reminiscent of Nagy’s first year as the team’s head coach, but if the early returns continue to trend in the right direction, Johnson’s reputation as one of the best offensive minds in football will be cemented. The work the first-year head coach was able to do in 2025 shouldn’t be overlooked, especially following a slow start to the season. Getting the most out of a young quarterback was his most important task, but the way he rebuilt the offensive line and drastically reshaped the running game might have been equally impressive. Chicago went from having one of the worst offensive lines in football to one of the best. Although two of their projected starters won’t be in the lineup for 2026, there’s reason to believe that Johnson and offensive line coach Dan Roushar will find a way…

full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 10: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball against Kingsley Enagbare #55 of the Green Bay Packers during an NFL wild card playoff game at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. D’Andre Swift is in the final year of the three-year, $24 million contract he signed with the Chicago Bears in 2024, and before last season, no one would have predicted he’d still be in Chicago. Most of the guaranteed money was paid out over the first two years, and it was just always assumed they’d cut him loose before this season. But he really took to Ben Johnson’s offense last year, and cutting him was never an option. He did so well in 2025 that last week general manager Ryan Poles was asked about a possible contract extension for the 27-year-old Swift. “Yeah, it’s definitely something we need to look at, and we will look at,” Poles said . “I think he’s done a great job. I love his approach this offseason. He looks amazing, and it’s his second year in the system, too. I think the combination of having EB [last year’s running backs coach Eric Bieniemy] and [this year’s RB coach Eric] Studsville has been awesome for him. So I like where he’s at right now.” In 2026, Swift’s cap hit is about $8.8M, which places him 12th among running backs, and his $8M per year average is tied for 19th. I think a two-year extension in the same ballpark is a possibility, but they may wait a while to see how this season goes to ensure it makes sense in the big picture. “This is where this job gets tough, is really trying to figure out how you want to allocate everything, not only for now, but into the future,” Poles continued. “So we’ll have those conversations and see where we want to go with it. title: Caleb Williams, Ben Johnson, Chicago Bears about to take fans on a fun ride
summary: I was writing some articles after the 53-man roster was announced and discussing how I have several concerns about the Chicago Bears defense, mostly the defensive line. A handful of fans on social media and in the comments section decided to voice their opinions that I am too negative. And truth be told, I probably […]
full_text: LAKE FOREST, ILLINOIS - JUNE 04: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears talks with head coach Ben Johnson during Chicago Bears OTA Offseason Workout at Halas Hall on June 04, 2025 in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images I was writing some articles after the 53-man roster was announced and discussing how I have several concerns about the Chicago Bears defense, mostly the defensive line. A handful of fans on social media and in the comments section decided to voice their opinions that I am too negative. And truth be told, I probably am. Being a Bears fan with this much failure over the last 35 years will do that to a person. But I am excited about the future here with Ben Johnson, and certainly excited about the future of Caleb Williams. But my negativity doesn’t reflect them or the offense in any way. My negativity is about trying to win a Super Bowl and the moves the Bears made (or mostly did not make) that make me think that goal is still out of reach in 2026. That’s what frustrates me. But with the dawn of a new season upon us, let’s not focus on the negatives; I’m sure I will have plenty of columns that voice my frustrations at one point or another. But let’s focus on the positives about where this team is, and where it’s going. Because if we are being honest, this should be the most excited you have been for a team entering a season since September of 1986. That’s right. This is the most exciting start to a season since 1986. This is better than 2019. This is better than 2007. In both 2007 and 2019, the Bears were coming off great seasons, but there were quarterback problems. Even when you look at the coaches. Matt Nagy did fairly well here. Obviously, Lovie Smith did very well here. But with either of those two coaches, were you ever 100% certain the Bears had an elite coach? A good coach? I’m sure many did, but did you ever think either of those coaches was one of the top three in the league? This is a totally different world. The Bears have, at minimum, a top-10 coach in the league; many experts would already put Ben Johnson in the top 5. And guess what? He’s pretty new at this, and he’s only getting better. Then there is Caleb Williams. I’ve been on the Caleb Williams bandwagon since the beginning (the beginning being the horrible start to the 2023 season). Perhaps it’s my jaded views of Chicago Bears quarterbacks, but I had him approaching the top 10 QBs in the league after last season, but when you look around the league, he’s almost at a consensus of already being in the top 10. How far can Caleb Williams fly this year? If everything goes the way Ben Johnson sees it, Williams is going to be in the top 5. He’s going to be in the same breath as Mahomes, Allen, Jackson, Stafford, and Burrow. He’s going to start becoming a regular conversation as part of the MVP race every season. Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams have changed the entire dynamic of the Chicago Bears franchise, and it’s incredibly awesome that we’ve arrived. Because of those two, the Chicago Bears will always have a place at the table. How many teams do you consider to have a top-10 QB and a top-10 coach in the NFL? Let’s take a look. Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes are one. Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson have new coaches. Joe Burrow has Zac Taylor, and Taylor is not at that level. Matthew Stafford and Sean McVay are two. I think you need to put Justin Herbert and Jim Harbaugh there. That’s three. You can’t put Schottenheimer there with Dak Prescott. You could make the argument that Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel are both there. That’s four. And then there’s Caleb and Ben. That’s five. What does that group of 5 have in common? Harbaugh and Herbert have been to the playoffs both years together. Maye and Vrabel made it in their only year; same with Caleb and Ben. McVay and Stafford have made it 4 of 5 years, and the one year they missed, Stafford missed 8 games. Mahomes and Reid made it 7 consecutive years and won three of five Super Bowl appearances. What am I trying to say? When you have a great coach and a great QB, you make the playoffs almost every year. That’s what the Chicago Bears are entering. Now, the roster may still need some TLC to get it to a point where it’s truly contending for a Super Bowl, but the Chicago Bears are entering a time where they should be a perennial playoff team every year. The Chicago Bears finally have a place at the table. Not only will the Bears be competing for playoff spots every year, but they are going to have the most explosive offense any living fan has ever seen. This offense is only getting better. Luther Burden and Colston Loveland are about to become elite weapons. Rome Odunze and D’Andre Swift have established themselves. Ben Johnson won’t let the offensive line be bad. Ever. This offense is going to be elite every year with the coach and QB combo. It’s going to be fun. Real fun. It’s going to be like something we’ve never experienced. NFL experts are going to do film studies on this offense. Ben Johnson’s coaching tree will become a thing like Sean McVay’s has. Nine times in Bears history has a QB thrown for over 3,000 yards and 20 TDs. Caleb Williams owns two of those in two seasons. He’s going to rewrite the Chicago Bears passing records. Ben Johnson is going to rewrite the Chicago Bears’ records for offense. Heck, Ben Johnson may become one of the top 10 most winning coaches in the history of the franchise THIS season. It’s a golden time to be a Chicago Bears fan. We are entering an era that we’ve never experienced. This is going to be new to all of us. But it’s going to be really f’ing fun. So buckle up, Bears fans. The Chicago Bears are no longer an NFL doormat. They are going to consistently be one of the better teams in the league. This is what Bears fans have wanted since Mike Ditka was carried off the field at the Louisiana Superdome, and it’s hard to imagine that the dream has become a reality. Enjoy it. Not just last season. Not just this season. But every season. Enjoy it. Enjoy all of it. Embrace the greatness we are about to witness year in and year out. The Chicago Bears have arrived. Bears fans are excited. TV Networks are excited. Roger Goodell is excited. Packers fans aren’t. As Jerry Seinfeld once said, “That’s a shame.” Embrace it all. I have. What a time to be alive.

MVP Offensive Player of the Year Defensive Player of the Year Offensive Rookie of the Year Defensive Rookie of the Year Coach of the Year Protector of the Year Super Bowl LXI Bryan Orenchuk: For Protector of the Year, I’m going with Penei Sewell of the Detroit Lions. Switching over to the LT spot will draw even more attention to the big fella from Oregon. I think he excels in the new role and plays a massive part in Jahmyr Gibbs’ dominant season. Josh Sunderbruch: It would send an interesting signal for the award to go to the highest-paid center in the league, so Tyler Linderbaum of the Las Vegas Raiders is my choice. If he’s able to keep Justin Herbert upright, that should go a long way toward individual and team success. Mongo Peanut: Keep it in Chicago with Darnell Wright. The kid is as talented as anyone in the league and puts it all together this year. Gary Baugher Jr.: Penei Sewell will get a lot of love after switching to left tackle and continuing to play at an All-Pro level. Erik Duerrwaechter: Joe Thuney is the first-ever recipient of the award. And I don’t see another OL who’s as capable of playing at such a high level between multiple positions if needed. Frankly, it should be renamed the Joe Thuney Award. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: If the Philadelphia Eagles Lane Johnson is healthy, I think the media will vote him as the winner. Besides being a really, really good right tackle, at 36 years old he’s on the back 9 of his career, so this would be a nice nod to recognize the greatness of the grizzled vet. Jeff Berckes: We’re all the winners now that the NFL has created this award. I think voters were wise in choosing Joe Thuney for the first-ever award last year, showing it wasn’t just going to be a left tackle every year. However, I think they’ll go that direction this season, and I really like the Tampa Bay Buccaneers Tristan Wirfs to take it home this year. He’s in his prime, and if he strings together a healthy season, I like his odds. Superfans: At first, we were thinking this is a situation where voters could split between the two Chicago All-Pros, which could hurt their individual chances at winning, but then we realized the greatness of Thuney and Wright will be so massive in 2026 that these two might be the only two offensive linemen receiving votes at all. So we’re predicting a tie. Who is your pick for 2026 Coach of the Year?

title: 2026 NFC North Season Preview and Prediction: The Bears will repeat
summary: The 2026 NFL regular season kicks off on Wednesday, which means that meaningful football is almost here! Although the offseason always feels like it drags on forever, once training camp kicks off, the preseason flies by.  Last season, the NFC North was the only division in football with all four teams finishing above .500. While […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 7: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears and Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers meet following an NFL football game at Lambeau Field on December 7, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season kicks off on Wednesday, which means that meaningful football is almost here! Although the offseason always feels like it drags on forever, once training camp kicks off, the preseason flies by. Last season, the NFC North was the only division in football with all four teams finishing above .500. While teams like the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings disappointed, the Chicago Bears surprised, and the Green Bay Packers met preseason expectations. Following a relatively mellow offseason for all four teams, the primary focus will be health moving into the regular season. Aside from some coordinator and assistant changes, each team will return large portions of its coaching staff and roster. With another tight race to the finish anticipated, we’ll dive into the most notable moves that each team made this offseason, along with an optimistic and pessimistic view heading into the season—all of that and more in the 2026 installment of our NFC North Season Preview. Chicago Bears (12-5) 1st Place (2nd Seed) Key Additions: S Coby Bryant, LB Devin Bush, S Dillon Thieneman (1st Round Pick), WR Kalif Raymond, C Garrett Bradbury Key Departures: WR DJ Moore, C Drew Dalman, S Kevin Byard, LB Tremaine Edmunds, DT Gervon Dexter Sr. Despite a surprising NFC North title and a thrilling playoff victory, general manager Ryan Poles and the Bears played it safe for the first time in a while this offseason. While the acquisition period focused on speed, they lost several leaders in the process. Trading Moore (considering his drop-off in production) was necessary, but not inconsequential. Dalman’s retirement was a tough blow, and replacing him with Bradbury, at least in the short term, is a noticeable downgrade. The team decided to remake its safety room, allowing both Byard and Jaquan Brisker to walk in free agency. Adding Bryant and Thieneman gives them a more versatile, athletic group that fits Dennis Allen’s scheme better. The issue is that Bryant was hurt early in camp and might not play in 2026, throwing their plan into chaos. Along the same lines of better scheme fits, swapping out Edmunds for Bush should pay off, although the defensive line and their lack of run support are cause for concern when looking at Bush’s lack of size. Overall, this wasn’t the type of offseason many fans expected, and, more importantly, their lack of action along the defensive line has many questioning whether they’re built for a Super Bowl run, especially after trading away Dexter shortly after the conclusion of the preseason. Reseason(s) For Optimism: Caleb Williams and Ben Johnson In Year 2 Should Provide Top 3-5 Results For the first time since the Marc Trestman era, the Bears’ offense looked like a successful modern-day unit that could score on anyone. That’s something fans have longed for, and the hope is that with another year of experience under their belts, the results will continue to trend in the right direction. There’s no denying that Williams needs to find more consistency on a down-to-down basis in Year 3, though. For as many “explosives” as the offense produced last season, there was still plenty left out on the field, especially on the drives they couldn’t score. While explosive plays will always be a focus for Johnson and his offensive coaching staff, the urgency to find more early-game success to establish a rhythm will be key to getting them into the Top 3-5 conversation. That said, they weren’t far off in Year 1, and there’s little reason to doubt that they can get there in 2026. Reason(s) For Concern: Will A Conservative Approach Along The Defensive Line Cost Them A Super Bowl Run? It’s safe to say that the Bears were one of the league’s surprise teams a year ago. No matter how they got there, going from worst to first is not an easy accomplishment, especially with a playoff victory sprinkled into last season’s magical run. Even so, their flaws were obvious, and despite having plenty of financial flexibility, at least on paper, general manager Ryan Poles approached the offseason with a sense of caution that wasn’t expected. Every team in the league is flawed, but most contenders attempt to fix those flaws during the offseason. Despite an unsustainable number of takeaways that helped keep the defense afloat, their lack of pass rush and run-stopping ability in the trenches was a notable flaw. Instead of throwing more resources at the problem, Johnson and his staff have spent the offseason insisting that coaching, better health, and players that fit the scheme will be the difference. The NFL is a copycat league, and the blueprint laid out by the previous two Super Bowl winners has a clear three-deep defensive line with top-end talent and plenty of depth. At least on paper, the Bears don’t have either, which could be the difference between a potential Super Bowl run and falling short. Detroit Lions (11-6) 2nd Place (6th Seed) Key Additions: C Cade Mays, RT Blake Miller (1st Round Pick), DE D.J. Wonnum, RB Isiah Pacheco, CB Roger McCreary Key Departures: LT Taylor Decker, RB David Montgomery, CB Terrion Arnold, LB Alex Anzalone, DE Al-Quadin Muhammad Right, wrong, or indifferent, it’s clear that the Lions treated 2025 as an exception rather than the rule. While they allowed some key players to walk in free agency, in addition to releasing Decker and trading Montgomery, the focus on the trenches was clear from the start. The first step was to fix their offensive line, which they hope to have done by adding Miller and Mays to the starting five. In addition, they added some high-upside, low-cost free agents like Wonnum, Pacheco, McCreary, and Christian Izien in free agency. Not listed in the key additions is second-round edge rusher Derrick Moore, who should see plenty of time opposite Aidan Hutchinson, even if on a rotational basis. Reality is, the Lions still have a stacked roster with plenty of talent. Injuries played a big role in their last-place finish, but the sportsbooks and analysts are bullish on their 2026 prospects alike. Their overall roster talent is not in question, but without better health among key players, their lack of impact on the move might look bad in hindsight. That’s where they are hoping better coaching and a new offensive coordinator, Drew Petzing, can flip the script. Reason(s) For Optimism: The Lions Remain The NFC North’s Most Talent-Rich Roster Whether you’ve tracked the NFL’s Top 100 or simply looked at different rankings from analysts, there’s no denying how talented the Lions are on paper. Offensively, you’d be hard-pressed to find many units better than them, even if you’re lower on quarterback Jared Goff than the consensus. Defensively, they have some questions, but assuming that the safety duo of Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch can return to full health this season, there’s a strong argument to be made for Detroit having a potential Top 5-7 defense. Assuming that new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing can get the offense back on track, the optimism surrounding the Lions for 2026 is warranted and very much real. Reason(s) For Concern: The Secondary’s Health and Cornerback Depth Talent on paper is one thing, but being healthy enough to play the majority of the season is another. We saw that exact situation with the Lions last season, when it seemed like every member of their secondary was dropping like flies as the season progressed. Despite the rash of injuries, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard did an outstanding job of rallying the troops, especially as a first-year coordinator. With that in mind, the team has invested quite a bit at safety, and even with the improved depth of Chuck Clark and Izien, this defense can reach its potential only…

title: Chicago Bears Rivalries Logo Glow-Up was the Star of the Reveal
summary: Have you seen the Chicago Bears’ new “Rivalries” uniforms put out by Nike? My first reaction was that they finally found a good pairing for that orange helmet they came out with a couple years ago. It’s got some fun wrinkles – the vertical stripes, the orange pants, awesome socks. The patch… yeah, sure, let’s […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES - NOVEMBER 7: Quarterback Sid Luckman #42 of the Chicago Bears runs past end Tom Fears #55 of the Los Angeles Rams during a game played on November 7, 1948 at the Los Angeles Coliseum in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Vic Stein /Getty Images) Have you seen the Chicago Bears’ new “Rivalries” uniforms put out by Nike ? My first reaction was that they finally found a good pairing for that orange helmet they came out with a couple years ago. It’s got some fun wrinkles – the vertical stripes, the orange pants, awesome socks. The patch… yeah, sure, let’s throw a patch on there, I guess. We’ll wait to give an official verdict when they play a game with these new duds, but they pass the initial test. Sure. It's a fun uniform concept with some good history elements. Finally found a better use of the orange helmet. #Bears https://t.co/vXLN0M3YRq — Jeff Berckes (Motivated) (@gridironborn) August 25, 2026 However, the real headliner isn’t even on the jersey – it’s the glow-up Nike gave the best logo in team history from the 1940s and 1950s. The bear on top of a giant orange football… or a tiny bear on a regular-sized football? Open to interpretation. Either way, the Bears started using that logo near the end of their greatest stretch in franchise history, led by Hall of Fame quarterback Sid Luckman paired with Hall of Fame coach George Halas. I say glow up because Nike smartly added “CHICAGO” inside the football, and the result is perfection. The Bears used that old logo as their primary marker for a generation before they adopted a white “C” to put on the side of their helmets in 1962. The white C turned orange in 1974 and is used to this day as the primary logo on helmets. The current bear head arrived in 1999 as the secondary logo, taking over as the primary for merchandise (but not the helmet, unfortunately) starting in 2023. I’ll save my discussion for another day on the need to refresh the brand every generation or two so that you can revisit eras like Nike did with this upcycled logo. It’s a lonely hill I’ll defend some other time. For now, I just want to reflect on this awesome logo and what it could mean to us Bears fans in the future. The “Rivalries Logo” enters the scene on the eve of the most anticipated season in quite some time. Chicago has been chasing the combination of elite coaching and quarterback play since Luckman and Halas left the sidelines. While we’ve only read the first chapter of the Ben Johnson-Caleb Williams book, most Bears fans agree that it is going to be a page turner. If this Johnson-Williams pairing takes the Bears back to the promised land, this logo will be associated with this newfound success. Much of the new gear that people will buy and wear during this stretch will feature this new logo. It will be in pictures and videos of fans cheering big victories. It will become part of the backdrop and good vibes will follow when Bears fans see the logo in the wild. Maybe I’m stretching here. Maybe I’m wish-casting, trying to pull some magic from a bygone era forward to the modern day. Maybe there isn’t any significance to the timing of a fresh logo besides the hit to my bank account over the next few months. But maybe, just maybe, this all adds up to something special on the lakefront. Put the ball on the tee and let’s ****ing go.

full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 29: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears looks on from the sideline during an NFL preseason game against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on August 29, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. We’ve been running through all our picks the last couple of days, and next up is Coach of the Year. Click the link below for any you may have missed. MVP Offensive Player of the Year Defensive Player of the Year Offensive Rookie of the Year Defensive Rookie of the Year Coach of the Year Protector of the Year Super Bowl LXI Bryan Orenchuk: I’m going with Ben Johnson. He wants records broken on offense – we’ll see records broken on offense and one of the most explosive offenses this century as the Chicago Bears firmly establish themselves as contenders under his leadership. Josh Sunderbruch: I want it to be Johnson, but I think it’s going to be Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers. Donald Gooch: Ben Johnson probably should have won it last year, but this year he leads the Bears to a second-division win in the toughest division in football, and he cements himself as one of, if not the, top offensive minds in football. Sam Householder: DeMeco Ryans – The Houston Texans have a very good team, and I think they could break through for a season that turns a lot of heads. Mongo Peanut: Kyle Shanahan. I think he’s going to go toe-to-toe with McVay and end up winning the division with a more flawed roster. This alone should win him the right. TJ Starman: Jesse Minter is my choice for coach of the year. I don’t think there’s an obvious team that was in the depths last season that will rise up this year, but Minter should be able to revitalize a talented Baltimore Ravens roster and get the most out of them. Erik Duerrwaechter: I’d argue Ben Johnson was snubbed last year in his first-ever season as a head coach. In year two, the league will learn to fear and appreciate him for the greatness he’s capable of achieving. Gary Baugher Jr.: Always the toughest to forecast because usually it goes to a coach who facilitated a turnaround with a bad team. So, of the new hires (or previous coaches who find themselves on new teams), I like the situation John Harbaugh is in. The defense is a top-half unit overall, and if he can unlock Dart more, I can see a 9-10 win season from the Giants with their 4th-place schedule. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: Minter will take the Ravens from a sub .500 team back to the playoffs, which is the kind of thing voters look for. Jeff Berckes: Sometimes this goes to the coach of a purely dominant team, but so often it goes to a coach that exceeds expectations. As if the media wasn’t wrong in their preseason forecast, and it was an amazing coaching job that lifted the team up. The NFC South has the following over/under win expectations: Panthers 6.5, Saints 7.5, Falcons 7.5, and Buccaneers 8.5. Someone has to win this division, and I’d be willing to put a dollar on the Saints emerging and Kellen Moore taking it home. Superfans: Honestly, the only negative surrounding Ben Johnson is a lack of facial hair, but we think the voters will overlook that and pick him after he leads the Bears to back-to-back NFC North titles. Who is your pick for 2026 Coach of the Year?

title: Ted Karras’ assessment of Bengals training camp should have fans paying attention
summary: There are the things NFL players say during training camp, and then there are the things that actually make you stop and listen. Ted Karras may have provided a little bit of the latter. Karras was once again named one of the Cincinnati Bengals‘ team captains for 2026, marking the fifth consecutive season that the […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) shares words with center Ted Karras (64) Ofer being sacked in the third quarter of the NFL Week 7 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Atlanta Falcons at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Sunday, Oct. 23, 2022. The Bengals won 35-17. Mandatory Credit: Sam Greene-The Enquirer Atlanta Falcons At Cincinnati Bengals Nfl Week 7 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There are the things NFL players say during training camp, and then there are the things that actually make you stop and listen. Ted Karras may have provided a little bit of the latter. Karras was once again named one of the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ team captains for 2026, marking the fifth consecutive season that the veteran center has held the honor. And considering how much football Karras has seen during his time in Cincinnati, his assessment of this year’s training camp is worth paying attention to. “This has probably been the toughest camp Coach Taylor has run in my five years here,” Karras said. That’s quite a statement. Five years is a long enough sample size to know what a Zac Taylor training camp typically looks like. Karras has experienced the good camps, the frustrating camps, the camps that produced legitimate optimism and the camps that ultimately didn’t translate into the kind of season the Bengals wanted. So when he says this was the toughest one, Bengals fans should probably take notice. But the most important part of Karras’ comments wasn’t necessarily the first sentence. It was what came next. “And I think we have a team that can handle that. We’re doing all the right things.” The Bengals Are Supposed to Be Tested There’s a natural temptation during training camp to focus on whether a team looks good. Who’s making plays? Which position group is winning? Who is standing out? Which rookie is generating buzz? Those things matter, but there’s another question that becomes increasingly important as the season approaches: Can this team handle adversity? That’s particularly relevant for the Bengals. Cincinnati doesn’t need another team that looks good when everything is going right. The Bengals need a team capable of surviving the grind of a 17-game season, handling injuries, responding to losses, and remaining focused when expectations get high. That’s where Karras’ comments become particularly interesting. He didn’t say the Bengals survived the toughest camp Taylor has put them through. He said they can handle it. There’s a difference. Karras Has Seen This Movie Before Karras isn’t some newcomer trying to establish himself in Cincinnati. He’s been through five training camps under Taylor. He’s been in the locker room for multiple playoff pushes. He’s been one of the team’s most consistent voices and has been selected as a captain every season he’s been with the Bengals. That continuity gives his comments more context. When Karras says the team has been “grinding,” he’s speaking from experience. And there’s another reason his perspective matters: the center position essentially gives him a front-row seat to the personality of the football team. He’s involved in every offensive snap. He’s communicating with Joe Burrow. He’s working with the offensive line. He’s dealing with the physicality of the defensive front. If the team isn’t practicing with the right level of intensity, a veteran center is going to know it. Apparently, that’s not an issue this year. This Is What Leadership Is Supposed to Look Like It’s also fitting that these comments came as Karras was once again named a captain. Cincinnati’s 2026 captaincy group contains a mixture of established leaders and new voices. Burrow and Ja’Marr Chase remain offensive pillars, while Karras provides the veteran presence in the middle. DJ Turner II, Bryan Cook and Dexter Lawrence II bring new leadership to the defensive side, while Evan McPherson represents special teams. Karras is the connective tissue. And perhaps that’s why his comments are more encouraging than a generic “we’re ready” quote. He’s not selling the idea that the Bengals are talented. Everyone knows they’re talented. He’s talking about work. “We’ve been grinding.” That’s the message you want coming from a veteran captain heading into a season in which the Bengals have made it abundantly clear that their expectations are much higher than simply making the playoffs. The Hard Part Is About to Begin Of course, none of this guarantees anything. Training camp isn’t the regular season. Being prepared to handle adversity doesn’t mean adversity won’t expose weaknesses. And ultimately, the Bengals will have to prove Karras right when the games actually count. But that’s precisely why his comments are encouraging. The Bengals aren’t talking about avoiding difficult circumstances. They’re talking about being prepared for them. That’s a subtle distinction, but an important one. The Bengals have the quarterback. They have elite offensive weapons. They have invested heavily in the defensive side of the football. They have added veteran leadership and young talent. Now they’re trying to build the kind of team that can survive everything that comes with being a legitimate contender. And according to one of the most experienced voices in the locker room, they’ve spent the offseason doing exactly that. Five years into his Cincinnati tenure, Ted Karras knows what a Bengals training camp looks like. He says this one was the toughest. And he says this team can handle it. Now comes the part where the Bengals have to prove him right.
author: Anthony Cosenza

title: Erick All isn’t thinking about his injury history ahead of his regular-season return
summary: Erick All has the potential to be a talented pass-catching tight end in the NFL. That’s why the Bengals selected him in the 2024 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, he hasn’t been able to really show it because he’s been injured throughout much of his young career in the league and in college football as well, which […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals tight end Erick All Jr. (83) stretches for a pass during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Erick All has the potential to be a talented pass-catching tight end in the NFL. That’s why the Bengals selected him in the 2024 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, he hasn’t been able to really show it because he’s been injured throughout much of his young career in the league and in college football as well, which is why he fell to them in the fourth round. All dealt with a back injury in 2022, and then tore his ACL in his right knee in 2023, missing the second half of the season. Then, in his rookie season, he tore the same knee again, which cost him the rest of 2024 and the entire 2025 season thanks to complications that required a second surgery. Now, he’s back and cleared to play in his third season. He’s not dwelling on the past, though. “Not really thinking about it. Like now, it kind of gets you, but when you’re out there, you kind of forget about that part of it, and you just play,” All said in an interview with Fox 19’s Gabi Sorrentino . Erick All Jr. hasn't played a regular season game in almost two years after tearing his ACL his rookie season…after a long recovery, the Bengals Tight End is ready to take the field with no limitations next Sunday. #Bengals @FOX19 pic.twitter.com/Dv4y0JrDCb — Gabi Sorrentino (@GSorrentinoTV) September 6, 2026 All’s spot on the 53-man roster, as long as he came into the season healthy, was really never in doubt. However, with so many mouths to feed in this offense, including Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, it’ll be interesting to see what kind of role he plays in the offense, and how that role evolves. All hopes to make it through an entire season for the first time since his 2021 season with Michigan, when he led the Wolverines in receptions with 38 catches for 437 yards and two touchdowns. He played in 13 games with eight starts that season. “Individually, just making it out of the season healthy, and really, that’s all I care about, to be honest,” said All. “I don’t care about anything else. I mean, as long as I’m doing good and we win games, then that’s all I really care about.” With Mike Gesicki, Drew Sample, and rookie Jack Endries on the roster to go with the talent at wide receiver, All will have his work cut out for him. Hopefully, he achieves his goal and helps the Bengals get back into the playoffs.
